Gabriela Saldana is a 23-year-old Florida International University capstone student who was arrested on April 15, 2026 in Miami-Dade County and charged with making written threats to kill or do bodily harm under Florida law. The arrest stemmed from a single message she posted in a 215-student WhatsApp group chat where classmates were discussing a Friday capstone-presentation event scheduled for FIU's Ocean Bank Convocation Center. Riffing on a widely-circulated social-media meme in which users sarcastically address Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and ask him to bomb a place they don't want to attend, Saldana wrote: "Netanyahu, if you can hear me, drop some bonbons for us Capstone students in Ocean Bank Convocation Center." A follow-up message — quoted by police in court as "There's going to be a bomb in the Ocean Bank Convocation Center and it was going to be Jonathan's fault" — was also entered into the record by detectives. After classmates expressed concern she replied: "I made a dumb joke that should not have been made."

She was arraigned April 16, 2026 in Miami-Dade County bond court before Judge Mindy S. Glazer, who set her bond at $5,000. Glazer found insufficient probable cause for the statutory "with prejudice" enhancement that would have classified the offense as a hate crime, but allowed the underlying written-threats charge to proceed. FIU stated publicly that she had made "a credible and imminent threat of violence at a planned university event."

Supporters and civil-liberties commentators have framed the prosecution as a politically-motivated criminalization of obvious satire — Saldana's joke targeted Netanyahu, not her classmates, and used "bonbons" rather than "bombs" as part of the meme's recognizable code. The case has been compared to the U.K. "#TwitterJokeTrial" Paul Chambers prosecution (2010) and to other recent U.S. arrests of students for online speech critical of Israel during the post-October-7 enforcement wave. Critics note that the prosecution comes amid a sharp uptick in prosecutions of pro-Palestinian student speech across U.S. campuses.

Aurelio Luis Perez-Lugones is a 61-year-old systems engineer and information technology specialist from Laurel, Maryland who held a Top Secret / Sensitive Compartmented Information security clearance while working as a Pentagon contractor. Beginning in October 2025 he is alleged to have taken screenshots of classified intelligence reports — some related to an unspecified foreign country — pasted them into Microsoft Word documents and other applications to obscure his unauthorized access, printed them, and brought them home. Documents marked SECRET were later recovered from a lunchbox in his car and from his basement.

Federal prosecutors allege he passed the materials to Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson, who co-wrote and contributed to at least five articles based on the information on October 31, November 11, and December 8, 2025, and January 6 and January 9, 2026. The leaked material informed Natanson's coverage of the Trump administration's reshaping of the federal government. Phone messages between Perez-Lugones and the reporter included him writing, "I'm going quiet for a bit … just to see if anyone starts asking questions," after sending one document.

He was arrested on January 8, 2026 and has remained jailed since. On January 22, 2026 a grand jury in the Eastern District of Virginia indicted him on five counts of unlawfully transmitting and one count of unlawfully retaining classified national defense information under the Espionage Act (18 U.S.C. §793). The indictment was announced by Attorney General Pamela Bondi and FBI Director Kash Patel. Six days after his arrest the FBI executed a pre-dawn search warrant at Natanson's home in Virginia and seized her phone, two laptops, a recorder, a portable hard drive, and a Garmin smartwatch — a seizure two federal judges (a magistrate and U.S. District Judge Anthony J. Trenga, ruling May 4, 2026) have since blocked DOJ from searching under the Privacy Protection Act.

The prosecution sits in the Reality Winner / Daniel Hale / Thomas Drake / John Kiriakou lineage of Espionage Act cases brought against federal workers who released information to journalists in the public interest. Each transmission count carries up to ten years in federal prison.

Julio Cesar Irungaray is a 56-year-old longtime Salt Lake City resident, father, and community activist, originally from Mexico, who had lived in Utah for more than 35 years. On June 24, 2026, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detained him outside his home as he returned from his night job, and he was placed in deportation proceedings while he was appealing an earlier removal order. His family said he has diabetes and feared for his safety in detention; roughly 90 supporters rallied for him the following evening, with more demonstrations planned. The Department of Homeland Security said he had prior convictions for driving under the influence and had entered the country in 1991.

Salah Sarsour, age 53, is a Palestinian-American lawful permanent resident and the president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, the largest mosque in Wisconsin. Born in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, he came to the United States in 1993 and has lived here for over thirty years. His wife and four adult children are U.S. citizens. He has no U.S. criminal record.

On the morning of April 1, 2026, nearly a dozen ICE agents surrounded his car as he left his Milwaukee home and detained him. He was transferred to a county jail in Indiana operating under ICE contract. The government invoked Section 237(a)(4)(C)(i) of the Immigration and Nationality Act — the so-called foreign policy deportability ground — claiming Secretary of State decision-making had determined his presence in the country poses a foreign-policy threat. The same statutory provision was used against Mahmoud Khalil, Rumeysa Ozturk, and other Palestinian-solidarity organizers in 2025-2026.

The Department of Homeland Security cited a juvenile-era Israeli military-court conviction from when Sarsour was 15 (allegedly throwing rocks at Israeli soldiers in the occupied West Bank) — a record the U.S. government has known about for thirty years. The Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Legal Fund of America, and ten Muslim civil-rights organizations issued a joint letter denouncing the arrest as targeting Sarsour for his Palestinian and Muslim background. Wisconsin elected officials and Milwaukee clergy joined calls for his release. His attorneys filed a habeas petition seeking immediate release.

Shamim Mafi is a 44-year-old Iranian national, a lawful permanent resident of the United States since 2016, who lived in Woodland Hills, California prior to her arrest. On the evening of April 18, 2026 she was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport by federal agents and charged in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California with a single count of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), 50 U.S.C. §1705. The prosecution alleges she brokered the sale of Iranian-manufactured drones, bombs, bomb fuses, and millions of rounds of ammunition for transfer to Sudan during that country's ongoing civil war.

If convicted she faces a statutory maximum of 20 years in federal prison. Her initial appearance was scheduled for the afternoon of April 20, 2026 in downtown Los Angeles. She is presumed innocent. The indictment was announced by U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bilal Essayli, a Trump-administration appointee with a politically prominent profile in Iranian-American policy circles.

The case is included in the NPPC database because IEEPA — the federal sanctions statute under which Mafi is charged — has been criticized by civil-liberties groups and Iranian-American legal-defense organizations for its disproportionate use against Iranian nationals and dual citizens in cases that often blend genuine export-control concerns with politically-coded prosecution. The defense bar has long argued that the statute's broad reach allows the government to criminalize conduct, including ordinary commercial transactions touching Iran, that would not be charged against defendants from other sanctioned jurisdictions. Mafi's prosecution will be watched as a test case for how aggressively the current administration pursues IEEPA enforcement against permanent residents of Iranian origin.

Spencer Anderson is a 24-year-old man from Clarkston, Michigan charged in February 2026 with three felony counts of malicious destruction of police property. Waterford Township police announced on February 23, 2026 that several Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR / Flock Safety) cameras in the township had been forcibly broken from their mounts and smashed. One of the still-functioning ALPRs captured the suspect's vehicle and plate at the scene; a nearby business's security camera recorded a person exiting the vehicle and striking two of the cameras with a blunt instrument. Anderson was arraigned February 27, 2026 in the 51st District Court in Waterford and released on a $500 cash bond. Each of the three counts carries up to four years in prison and a $5,000 fine, plus restitution for the roughly $10,000 in damaged equipment.

A probable-cause conference was set for March 11, 2026 with a preliminary examination scheduled for March 18, 2026. Supporters frame the case as anti-surveillance civil disobedience targeting one of the most widely deployed private ALPR systems in U.S. policing; prosecutors and Waterford police characterize it as malicious property destruction. The entry is neutral and notes both framings.

Robert Jacob Hoopes, 25, is an activist from Portland, Oregon with ties to the Quaker community. He was among the protesters who gathered regularly outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building in Portland in 2025 to protest the Trump administration's mass deportation campaign. During a protest in June 2025, Hoopes threw a rock that struck an ICE officer in the head, opening a gash over the officer's eye; he also used a stop sign as a battering ram causing approximately $7,000 in damage to the ICE facility. He was identified through FBI facial recognition technology. Under a plea agreement, Hoopes pleaded guilty to aggravated assault of a federal employee with a dangerous weapon; charges related to the property damage were dismissed. On June 11, 2026, U.S. District Judge Adrienne Nelson sentenced him to 30 months in federal prison plus three years of supervised release and ordered him to pay over $8,000 in restitution.

20-year-old U.S. citizen and Walmart employee arrested June 17, 2025 in Pico Rivera, California during the federal deployment to the Los Angeles area. Federal prosecutors charged him with assaulting a CBP agent during the protests against the immigration raids; bystander video circulated publicly disputed the government's account.

Daniel Jongyon Park, 32, was arrested June 4, 2025 at JFK Airport, charged in the Central District of California with providing and attempting to provide material support to a terrorist. Park purchased explosive components used by co-conspirator Guy Bartkus to manufacture a VBIED that detonated outside an IVF clinic in Palm Springs, killing the bomber and injuring 4. The attack was planned for over a year and linked to the anti-natalist Efilism movement. Park died in custody by suicide (jumping from a prison balcony) before legal proceedings concluded.

Ginovanni Joseph Brumbelow, 21, is an activist from Gresham, Oregon. On June 14, 2025 — No Kings Day, chosen to coincide with Donald Trump's birthday — he was arrested at a Portland protest against ICE immigration enforcement. He was charged with felony assault on a federal officer under 18 U.S.C. § 111(a)(1) and held approximately two days in federal custody before release pending trial. His case was among dozens arising from intensified federal prosecution of immigration-related demonstrators during the Trump administration's second term.

Jamison R. Wagner, 40, is a queer electrical engineer from Albuquerque, New Mexico, with a B.S. in electrical engineering and a partially completed master’s degree from the University of New Mexico, who previously worked at SolAero Technologies and Intel and co-authored research with Los Alamos National Laboratory. He was arrested on April 12, 2025 and charged with two federal counts of arson in connection with two property destruction actions in early 2025: on February 9, 2025, he allegedly set fire to the Tesla Albuquerque Showroom on the Santa Ana Pueblo in Sandoval County, leaving graffiti reading “Die Elon,” “Tesla Nazi Inc,” and swastika symbols, in apparent response to Elon Musk’s role in the Trump administration; and on March 30, 2025, he allegedly firebombed the Republican Party of New Mexico headquarters in Albuquerque, leaving graffiti reading “ICE=KKK.” FBI and ATF agents found eight assembled incendiary devices, improvised napalm materials, a stencil matching the GOP office graffiti, and a notebook containing plans for “violence against the regime” during a search of his home; DNA from a gin bottle left at the GOP office scene led to his identification. He was ordered held without bail and has remained in federal pretrial detention since April 2025. As of July 2026, he had not entered a plea, with trial scheduled for September 14, 2026 before District Judge Kea W. Riggs; he faces five to twenty years per count on two counts (up to forty years). FBI Director Kash Patel and Attorney General Pam Bondi characterized the case as “domestic terrorism.” Wagner identifies publicly as queer and bisexual and was listed in the “500 Queer Scientists” visibility campaign.

Mohammed Hoque is a 20-year-old Bangladeshi international student at Minnesota State University, Mankato. On March 28, 2025, plainclothes ICE officers followed his car as he returned home from a coding class and surrounded him at his home, telling him his student visa had been revoked. He was held in ICE custody for over a month. He had no criminal record; the only basis the government cited was social-media activity, including Instagram posts about violence against Palestinians in Gaza and a #FreePalestine hashtag in his Instagram bio.

His attorneys filed a habeas petition arguing his detention was First Amendment retaliation for his support of Palestinian human rights. On May 7, 2025, U.S. District Judge Jerry Blackwell of the District of Minnesota ordered his immediate release, finding that Hoques arrest aligns with the publicly stated executive policy of targeting social media users who express support for Palestinian human rights and criticize violence in Gaza. He was released on a $7,500 bond.

Mufid Fawaz Alkhader, 29, US citizen born in Iraq and living in Schenectady NY, was indicted February 4, 2025 for discharging a Kel-Tec shotgun into the air twice outside Temple Israel synagogue in Albany while shouting Free Palestine. Attempted to fire a third time but the shotgun jammed; then attempted to tear an Israeli flag from a flagpole. Stated he wanted to scare Zionists. Had a prior restraining order which prevented gun-shop purchase. Pleaded guilty; 120 months federal prison.

Salem Seleiman, 30, was sentenced December 4, 2025 to 24 months New York state prison for the May 20, 2021 antisemitic hate-crime assault in Times Square against a 29-year-old Jewish man attending a Pro-Israel rally; the victim was beaten, pepper-sprayed, kicked, and subjected to antisemitic slurs. Sixth defendant sentenced in connection with the incident; pleaded guilty September 29, 2025.

Tyler Robinson, 22, of Washington, Utah, is the man accused of fatally shooting conservative activist Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University in Orem on September 10, 2025. He was charged on September 16, 2025 with aggravated murder, felony discharge of a firearm, obstruction of justice, and witness tampering; Utah prosecutors are seeking the death penalty, alleging a politically motivated killing. He remains in custody and is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Xaelyn Dunbar, 19, was arrested in September 2025 and charged with making a terroristic threat over Facebook comments about a Charlie Kirk memorial vigil at the University of Texas at San Antonio, referencing his truck. He told police he was joking and was held in the Bexar County Jail on a 40,000-dollar bond.

Yaakub Ira Vijandre is a 38-year-old Filipino-American photojournalist, videographer, and longtime pro-Palestinian organizer based in the Dallas–Fort Worth area of Texas. He came to the United States from the Philippines with his family in 2001 at age 14, and has lived in the country lawfully since then; he is a recipient of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA). He has no criminal record. His photography and on-the-ground video coverage of pro-Palestinian protests in North Texas — circulated widely on Instagram and through Drop Site News, the MLFA, and other independent press channels — made him one of the most prolific visual chroniclers of the Palestine solidarity movement in the South.

In late 2023, according to his legal team, he was approached by the Federal Bureau of Investigation with a request that he become a confidential informant inside the pro-Palestinian movement in Texas. He declined. Over the following two years, he continued his photojournalism and his organizing work, including extensive documentation of the ICE detentions of other pro-Palestinian community members across the Dallas area in 2025.

On the night of October 6, 2025, Vijandre filmed a Richardson City Council meeting at which residents and organizers spoke against the ICE detention of a local Palestinian community leader. The next morning, October 7, 2025, ICE agents arrested him at gunpoint at his home in Richardson, Texas. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has stated that the basis for the detention and for the Department's attempt to revoke his DACA status is his social media activity — Instagram posts and likes critical of U.S. foreign policy, U.S. support for Israel, and U.S. immigration enforcement. He has not been charged with any crime.

He was initially held at the Bluebonnet Detention Center in Anson, Texas, where his attorneys and family could visit. On October 30, 2025, ICE transferred him approximately 1,000 miles away to the Folkston ICE Processing Center in Folkston, Georgia, a remote and overcrowded private facility operated by the GEO Group. His attorneys argued that the transfer was retaliatory and was designed to obstruct his access to counsel and to the press.

His legal team — including the Muslim Legal Fund of America, Asian Americans Advancing Justice–Atlanta, and Asian Americans Advancing Justice–AAJC — has filed a habeas corpus petition seeking his immediate release. They argue that his detention is unconstitutional retaliation for First Amendment-protected speech and journalism, and that the government's use of social media surveillance to strip a DACA recipient of his lawful status sets a dangerous precedent for the criminalization of pro-Palestinian and immigrant journalists. As of this writing he remains in ICE custody at Folkston, awaiting decisions on his habeas petition and his removal proceedings.

Bridget Irene Shergalis, 27, of Dayville CT, Palestine Action US member; co-defendant in the November 2023 Elbit Systems vandalism in Merrimack NH. She was charged with a second-degree felony of making a threat of terrorism, with bond set at 100,000 dollars. State prosecutors dropped the charge on February 25, 2025.

Casey Robert Goonan, 34, of Oakland and Pleasant Hill CA, ignited six Molotov cocktails inside a UC Berkeley UCPD patrol vehicle on June 1, 2024, attempted to firebomb the Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building/U.S. Courthouse in Oakland on June 11, 2024, and set additional fires on the UCB campus June 1/13/16 2024. Blogged photos under Student Intifada banner; admitted inspiration from Hamas Oct 7, 2023 attack. DOJ called him a domestic terrorist. Pleaded guilty; 235 months federal prison. Casey Goonan is a Palestine-solidarity activist who on July 2, 2024 set fire to a University of California Police Department vehicle parked on the UC Berkeley campus, in protest of UC investments in companies tied to Israel and the role of campus police in suppressing pro-Palestinian protest during the war in Gaza. He claimed the action publicly. He was arrested by federal authorities and pleaded guilty in 2025 to federal arson and use of fire to commit a federal felony. He was sentenced to approximately seven years in federal prison with the federal terrorism enhancement applied — among the longest sentences imposed on a U.S. anti-war activist in the post-October 7 Palestine solidarity wave.

Chase Payton Grijalva is a 30-year-old former U.S. Army mechanic from Portland, Oregon. Over a roughly two-week stretch in late May and early June 2024 he shot out 17 city red-light and speed-enforcement cameras across 12 separate incidents, beginning May 27, 2024 at NE Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard and Lloyd Boulevard. He was arrested on June 10, 2024 after a witness identified him near SE 122nd and SE Stark; after a Miranda warning he admitted to police that he had been shooting cameras for more than a week.

On Wednesday, March 4, 2026, Multnomah County Circuit Court Judge Andrew Lavin sentenced him to 24 months in Oregon state prison followed by five years of probation, with an additional five-year suspended prison term contingent on probation compliance, and ordered him to pay $55,548 in restitution. Total camera damage was estimated at roughly $500,000. He pleaded guilty to one count of unlawful use of a firearm, two counts of unlawful use of a weapon, and one count of first-degree criminal mischief.

Supporters frame the case as a disproportionate punishment for a sustained act of civil disobedience against municipal surveillance infrastructure and have flagged that arresting officers used force during the June 2024 arrest. Critics view it as a straightforward case of repeated firearm-related criminal mischief. The case is logged here because of the anti-surveillance protest framing in the public discussion; the entry is neutral and does not endorse either characterization.

Christopher K. Zelle, 37, indicted May 16, 2024 with two counts of Mob Action and felony aggravated battery for the UIUC Gaza encampment defense. Pleaded guilty to lesser; 4 days time served + 12 mo conditional discharge + 100 hours public service.

George A. Vassilatos, 25, indicted May 16, 2024 with felony Mob Action and misdemeanor obstructing for the UIUC Gaza encampment defense. Felony dismissed; misdemeanor guilty plea. 12 mo conditional discharge + 30 hrs community service.

Indicted March 12, 2024 on federal hate-crime charges. Acquitted - jury found insufficient evidence of religious or national bias motivation.

Donald Mark Johnson, 33, was arrested June 26, 2024 at the University of Pittsburgh Gaza divestment protest for aggravated assault and related charges. Pleaded guilty to lesser charges; 24 months probation.

Donald Jose-David Zepeda, age 35, of Maryland, a member of the climate group Declare Emergency, dumped red powder over the display case holding the U.S. Constitution in the Rotunda of the National Archives in Washington, D.C. on February 14, 2024, alongside co-defendant Jackson Green, to demand action on climate change. The cleanup cost more than $58,000 and closed the Rotunda for four days. He pleaded guilty on August 15, 2024 to felony destruction of government property and was sentenced on November 15, 2024 by Judge Amy Berman Jackson to 24 months in federal prison.

Elijah Michael Lane, 29, was charged May 3, 2024 with first-degree burglary, assaulting a public safety officer, fourth-degree assault, ESG/tear gas/mace use, and misdemeanors stemming from the Portland State University anti-Boeing/Israel-Gaza protest. All charges dismissed at disposition March 10, 2025.

Will Parzybok, 23, was charged May 3, 2024 with assaulting a public safety officer, unlawful use of a weapon, and interfering with a peace officer at the Portland State University anti-Boeing/Israel-Gaza protest. All charges dismissed February 10, 2025; paid $20 to Defense Fund PDX.

Hashem Younis Hashem Hnaihen, 43, Jordanian national residing illegally in Orlando, left letters at multiple Orange County FL locations June 25, 2024 threatening to explode everything here in whole America. Damaged a Wedgefield FL solar power facility on June 29, 2024; the targets supported Israel. Pleaded guilty; sentenced April 2025 to 72 months federal prison.

Hicham Talal, 24, was arrested February 26, 2024 for vandalizing a Webster Bank in West Hartford CT for its investments in Israeli weapons manufacturing. Charged with hate-crime-enhanced criminal mischief; charges dropped July 29, 2024 after public protest pressure.

Jackson George Green, age 27, of Utah, a member of the climate group Declare Emergency, dumped red powder over the display case holding the U.S. Constitution in the Rotunda of the National Archives on February 14, 2024, alongside co-defendant Donald Zepeda. He had earlier, on November 14, 2023, painted "Honor Them" in red on the wall beside the Augustus Saint-Gaudens Shaw 54th Regiment Memorial at the National Gallery of Art, causing about $706 in damage. He pleaded guilty in August 2024 and was sentenced on November 12, 2024 by Judge Amy Berman Jackson to 18 months in federal prison for the Archives action, with a 90-day sentence for the National Gallery action to run concurrently.

Jarrid Bailey Huber, 23, was arrested May 2, 2024 in Portland for starting a fire at a UPS distribution facility, stating UPS was financially supporting the Atlanta police training facility. Pleaded guilty January 14, 2025 to arson and criminal mischief; 10 days jail + 3 years probation.

Jeffrey Stevens, 41, of Fort Wayne IN, freelance journalist for The Arab American News, communicated threats online November 17-20, 2023. Posted to the CIA public website that he was going to shoot every government official in the head, and messaged Fort Wayne PD that he would kill every Jew in Fort Wayne. Pleaded guilty; 15 months federal prison with hate-crime motivation enhancement.

Jenny O'Connell-Nowain is a 41-year-old former preschool teacher from Redding, California with no prior criminal history. At a Shasta County Board of Supervisors meeting in November 2024 she briefly interrupted former supervisor Patrick Jones, who was criticizing the county elections office, then sat silently on the floor in front of the dais holding a political sign. She was charged with a misdemeanor under California Penal Code §403 (disrupting a public meeting).

After a weeklong jury trial in early 2026 she was convicted. Visiting Judge Thomas L. Bender (Madera County) offered her probation; the proposed conditions would have required her to follow Board-of-Supervisors meeting rules going forward. She refused, telling the court she could not in good conscience accept terms that conflicted with her First Amendment rights. On January 28, 2026 Judge Bender sentenced her to 90 days in the custody of the Shasta County Sheriff's Office, which she served as roughly 45 days of house arrest with an ankle monitor before being released in early March 2026. Her husband Benjamin lost his job over the family's protest activity. The case drew national attention as an early test of how aggressively local prosecutors can criminalize silent, sit-in–style protest at public meetings; Deputy DA Emily Mees prosecuted.

Sources: r/law (March 2026), The Guardian, Shasta Scout, KRCR, A News Cafe.

Karrem Nasr, 23, of New Jersey, was charged in late December 2023 by SDNY with attempting to join and provide material support to al-Shabaab, a designated FTO. Cited the October 7, 2023 attack as motivation. Pleaded guilty; sentenced to 60 months federal prison + 15 years supervised release.

Marquis Frasier, 27, said he was at the Public Safety Building "when the riots occurred" on May 30, 2020 in Rochester, NY. He allegedly admitted to spray painting, smashing the windows of a truck, breaking glass at the Court Exchange Building, and stealing drinks from a vending machine. He admitted to having a Molotov cocktail (a Cuervo bottle) which he tried unsuccessfully to light, then threw into the back window of a trailer. Frasier was already charged in Rochester City Court on June 22 with first-degree arson and other state charges. Charged but not tried federally.

Graham Ball, 26, March 2024 Boeing Heath OH blockade defendant. Pleaded guilty; ~30 days.

On January 18, 2023, during a multi-agency raid on the Stop Cop City forest encampment in the South River Forest near Atlanta, Georgia State Patrol officers shot and killed 26-year-old forest defender Manuel Esteban Paez Terán (Tortuguita). Georgia and DeKalb County prosecutors responded with the most aggressive use of state-level domestic-terrorism and RICO statutes against a U.S. protest movement in modern history: 42 forest defenders were charged under Georgia's domestic-terrorism statute (originally enacted in 2017 in response to white-supremacist mass shootings) for activities ranging from camping in the forest to attending a March 2023 music festival a mile from the construction site. The RICO case has remained largely stalled in pretrial proceedings; this database entry is for one of the small number of defendants who were denied bond or otherwise held in custody for meaningful periods before posting bail.

In September 2022 she pleaded guilty to possession of a Molotov cocktail and was sentenced to 18 months in federal prison, which she served at the Federal Medical Center at Carswell in Fort Worth, Texas.

On April 1, 2025, at the end of her federal sentence, she was taken into ICE custody for deportation to Chile. After several months in immigration detention she was deported and reunited with family in Chile, separated from her partner, family, and community in the United States.
Brittany Dawn Jeffrey, 31, of Little Rock AR, lead defendant in Jeffrey et al.; the Molotov cocktails were assembled at her residence. Pleaded guilty; 17 months federal prison + $529.30 restitution.

Emily Nowlin, 27, of Little Rock AR, was indicted December 14, 2020 in the Jeffrey et al. case for August 2020 Molotov-cocktail attacks on police vehicles at the Little Rock PD 12th Street Substation and Arkansas State Police Headquarters. Pleaded guilty; 18 months federal prison + $35,956.31 restitution.

Atlanta defendant prosecuted for the June 13, 2020 arson of the Wendy's restaurant at 125 University Avenue — the site where APD officer Garrett Rolfe had killed 27-year-old Rayshard Brooks the previous evening. The Wendy's fire became a defining image of the George Floyd uprising in Atlanta. Both defendants were charged with felony arson; both pled to lesser charges and received probationary sentences. Kingston was a co-defendant in the same proceeding.

Atlanta defendant prosecuted for the June 13, 2020 arson of the Wendy's restaurant at 125 University Avenue — the site where APD officer Garrett Rolfe had killed 27-year-old Rayshard Brooks the previous evening. White was identified via security footage and turned herself in.

Abdimanan Bana Habib, 21, of Fargo ND, threw rocks at police and attempted to light a Molotov cocktail during the May 2020 BLM protests. Charged October 21, 2020. Pleaded guilty; 4 months federal prison + 3 years supervised release + $2,500 restitution.

Abraham Elijah Jenkins, 26, of Charleston SC, was charged September 8, 2020 with civil disorder for the May 30, 2020 Charleston BLM protest. Pleaded guilty; 18 months federal prison + 36 months supervised release.

Tearra NaAsia Guthrie, 23, of Charleston, charged September 8, 2020 with civil disorder for the May 30, 2020 Charleston BLM protest. Pleaded guilty; 7 months federal prison (terrorism-enhancement-applied guideline cap of 5 years was avoided in plea). Died May 2022.

Adrian Wood, 21, was charged with one count of civil disorder in Wilmington, DE. Wood threw a brick through the back window of an occupied Wilmington police cruiser during an evening of protests and looting in the city's downtown area. Sentenced to time served (~18.6 months between arrest June 15, 2020 and judgment January 3, 2022).

Alexander Charles Pridgen, 18, of Greenville NC, threw a brick through a ground-floor window of the federal bankruptcy court during the May 31, 2020 BLM protest, then later vandalized the Greenville Police Station. Firearm charge added while indicted. Convicted; 15 months federal prison.

On May 28, 2020 as part of ongoing protests sparked by George Floyd's murder, Alexander Steven Heil, 24, joined and engaged with others to accelerate a fire in the Wells Fargo Bank building in south Minneapolis. Per defense filings, Heil "went to the Lake Street area to be part of the protest, drank too much and in a senseless, impulsive act while clearly under the influence of alcohol, threw a traffic cone into the existing fire." Sentenced to 30 months federal prison.

On May 31, 2020 following protests in Trenton, NJ, Justin Spry, 21, was seen on video with Killian Melecio and Kadeem Dockery attempting to set fire to a police car. Spry was arrested at the scene; Melecio and Dockery fled. Sentenced to 24 months federal prison plus 3 years supervised release.

Amanda R. Wolf, age 23, of Lombard IL, was arrested June 1, 2020 and charged with attempted terrorism and possession of an incendiary device after helping co-defendant Christian Frazee approach Lombard police squad cars with a Molotov cocktail, lighters, butane torches, and a bat. Pleaded guilty; 48 months Illinois state prison.

Christian Frazee, age 25, of Lombard IL, was arrested June 1, 2020 near the Lombard Municipal Complex and charged with attempted terrorism, possession of incendiary devices, and conspiracy to commit terrorism. Pleaded guilty; 120 months Illinois state prison.

Devinare Antwan Parker, 25, was charged in Seattle, WA with unlawful possession of a destructive device after he threw a 16-ounce can of beer through the window of a Seattle PD car, striking an officer in the face on May 31, 2020. When arrested he possessed an improvised firearm capable of firing shotgun shells. While being arrested he yelled that he had brought the firearm to kill police officers. Sentenced to 24 months federal prison.

Andrew Darnell Carlisle, 29, of Atlanta was arrested on two counts of felony criminal interference with government property and one count of misdemeanor rioting after state investigators accused him of vandalizing the Georgia Department of Public Safety headquarters during a racial justice protest in July 2020. He was among a group throwing stones and incendiary devices through windows and spray-painting graffiti. As of September 2023 he was also charged in the Stop Cop City RICO case with 61 others. Sentenced to 1 month in Georgia state prison.

Andrew Stegner, 19, of Lynchburg, VA was charged with throwing a projectile into an occupied building (felony) and rioting (misdemeanor) after his participation in a Lynchburg Black Lives Matter protest in May 2020. He was allegedly part of a group that threw rocks at a restaurant after it was accused of publishing a racist tweet. Acquitted of the felony but found guilty of misdemeanor rioting; sentenced to 6 months prison with a 5-month suspended sentence.

Andrew Salvarani Garcia-Smith, 32, was charged for the burning of the Market House in Fayetteville, NC on May 30, 2020. He was caught on video throwing a bottle of burning liquid into the Market House and the burning liquid spilled back onto him, setting his hair and clothes ablaze. Sentenced to 27 months federal prison.

Andrew Steven Faulkner, 24, of Beaverton OR, charged July 6, 2020 with assaulting federal officers using high-intensity lasers during the July 5-6, 2020 Portland federal courthouse protests. Possessed a sheathed machete at arrest. Pleaded guilty; 6 months detention + 3 years probation + 40 hours community service.

Anthony Richard Couse III, 51, of West Palm Beach, FL (homeless at time of arrest) was charged with two felonies and two misdemeanors following his participation in a West Palm Beach BLM protest on May 31, 2020. He allegedly challenged Deputy Police Chief Rick Morris to a fight and egged on demonstrators. Pled guilty to lesser charges of felony resisting arrest with violence and misdemeanor disorderly conduct; sentenced to 2 months Florida state prison plus 18 months probation.

Anthony David Ale Smith, 29, with co-defendants Carlos Matchett and Khalif Miller, indicted October 20, 2020 for the May 30, 2020 arson of a Philadelphia PD vehicle. Pleaded guilty June 6, 2023 to obstruction of law enforcement during civil disorder, several months after Philadelphia announced a $9.25 million police-response settlement. ~12 months federal prison. Anthony "Ant" Smith is a Black North Philadelphian indicted in October 2020 by Trump U.S. Attorney General William Barrs Department of Justice on federal charges arising from the May–June 2020 protests in Philadelphia following the police murder of George Floyd. He was one of five Philadelphians charged in a coordinated federal indictment alongside co-defendant Khalif Miller. He served substantial federal prison time and was released in August 2024. His support committee organized under the @FreeAntPHL handle on Twitter and Instagram.

Ayoub Tabri, 24, of Arlington, VA was charged for the arson of a Pennsylvania State Police SUV during civil unrest in Philadelphia on May 30, 2020. PSP placed two patrol SUVs at the on-ramp for I-676 to prevent protestors from accessing the highway; a group attacked the vehicles, shattering windows and stealing road flares, fire extinguishers, and "riot bags" of PSP-issued equipment. Tabri allegedly threw a lit road flare into K1-17, igniting a fire that engulfed the SUV. Tabri was wanted by the FBI Philadelphia Joint Terrorism Task Force prior to capture. Sentenced to 30 months federal prison.

On the night of May 28, 2020 Bailey Marie Baldus, 19, was caught on surveillance camera with co-defendants Mckenzy Ann Degidio Dunn and Samuel Elliot Frey at a St. Paul, MN health and nutrition store during the unrest after George Floyd's death. Charges against Baldus were dropped after her defense attorney argued she was in the building but did not participate.

Martino Andrews is an Ohio activist who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit arson for torching a county van during the May 30, 2020 George Floyd/BLM protests in Columbus, Ohio. His plea agreement recommended a sentence of 3.5 years in federal prison.

Martino Andrews, 22, of Cleveland, OH was charged with aggravated arson for setting a Cuyahoga County-owned van on fire during the May 30, 2020 protests in downtown Cleveland over the police killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis. Sentenced to 41 months federal prison plus $3,721.88 restitution.

Brian Jordan Bartels, 20, of Pittsburgh, attacked and vandalized a police car during the May 30, 2020 BLM protest. Charged June 9, 2020. Pleaded guilty; 1 day in custody + 6 months in a halfway house.

Bruce Thompson, 22, Gainesville GA Smallwood et al. co-defendant for the May/June 2020 police vehicle arson. Pleaded guilty; 14 months federal prison + 3 years supervised release + $3,678.17 restitution.

Dashun Martin, 23, was indicted June 17, 2020 in Gainesville GA along with co-defendants Jesse James Smallwood, Delveccho Waller Jr., Bruce Thompson, and Judah Coleman Bailey for conspiring to and committing arson of a police vehicle during the post-George Floyd protests. Pleaded guilty; 17 months federal prison + 3 years supervised release + $3,678.17 restitution.

Carlos Fugarte, 28, of Lakeland, FL was charged with written threat to kill after making comments encouraging people to blow up the local courthouse on a Facebook livestream of a Lakeland Black Lives Matter protest on May 31, 2020. Posting under the username "Woodboy Los," he issued a call to "Go to Bartow and blow up the courthouse." Sentenced to 1 month in Florida state prison plus 24 months probation.

Carlos Espriu, 23, of Palm Desert, CA was charged with attempted arson in the May 31, 2020 firebombing of the East Valley Republican Women Federated (EVRWF) office in La Quinta, CA. Espriu used a metal baseball bat to break windows at the EVRWF headquarters, then lit an improvised incendiary device of three bottles and tossed them through the windows before fleeing. He returned twice — once to retrieve the Molotovs, once to throw them, igniting a fire. Sentenced to 60 months federal prison plus $5,426 restitution.

Chelsie Eggers, 27, of Fargo, ND was charged with arming rioters, attempting to commit assault, rioting, and disobedience of public safety orders after she was arrested in connection with a protest related to the murder of George Floyd on May 30, 2020. Sentenced to 1 month in North Dakota state prison plus 1 year probation.

Christian Rea, 19, threw an explosive/incendiary device near a Naperville IL PD Special Response team vehicle and officers on June 1, 2020. The device exploded; 4 officers temporarily blinded and momentarily deafened. Pleaded guilty; 1 month federal prison.

Da'Jon Lengyel, 22, and Christopher Alan West damaged and destroyed by fire a Pittsburgh police vehicle and damaged a police officer's vehicle by hitting, kicking and stomping on its parts and joining others to destroy it by fire on May 30, 2020. Sentenced to 27 months federal prison.

In July 2020 in Portland, OR, Cody Beau Porter, 28, was charged with forcibly interfering with a federal officer for allegedly assaulting officers with a high-intensity laser during a protest related to police brutality and the murder of George Floyd. Case dismissed as part of a deferred resolution agreement.

Cody Michael Tarner, 23, of Hagerstown, MD, was indicted by a federal grand jury for burning two Supreme Court Police vehicles and attempting to burn a third on July 15, 2020. Tarner poured gasoline from a can into three Supreme Court Police vehicles, igniting two; he himself was engulfed in flames and suffered severe burns before a Supreme Court Police officer rendered first aid. One vehicle was destroyed, one damaged, the third did not catch fire. He was held without bond pending trial; tried unsuccessfully to plead insanity.

On May 31, 2020 Corey Cardale Gee, 28, of Tampa, FL was arrested for unlawful violation of emergency measures and burglary of an unoccupied structure during protests for George Floyd. He was seen breaking into a Marathon gas station. Sentenced to 8 months in Florida state prison.

Corey Smith, 24, gender non-conforming, with co-defendant Elaine Carberry, set fire to a marked NYPD Homeless Outreach Unit van on University Place at 4:35 a.m. July 15, 2020. Charged August 11, 2020. Pleaded guilty; 6 months federal prison.
Elaine Carberry, 36, with Corey Smith set fire to an NYPD Homeless Outreach van on July 15, 2020 in NYC. Charged August 11, 2020. Pleaded guilty; 6 months federal prison.

Cortez Lamont Edwards, 29, of Louisville, KY was charged as a felon in possession of a firearm. On September 23, 2020 Edwards went live on Facebook with an AR variant pistol with a non-extendible support brace and extended magazine. He stated he was requesting payment of $30,000 to shoot Louisville Metro PD officers responding to a disturbance in front of his residence. He had a 2019 felony conviction for trafficking in a controlled substance. ATF, HSI, U.S. Marshals, FPS, and LMPD executed a search warrant at his residence and recovered a Glock 19 9mm pistol. Sentenced to 30 months federal prison plus 2 years supervised release.

Courtland Renford, 20, was charged with arson after throwing a burning basket into Buffalo City Hall during weekend protests in Buffalo, NY in 2020. The government argued in detention pleadings that "Congress determines Renford setting fire to an empty building [is] an act of terrorism." Sentenced to 60 months federal prison.

Craig Michael Digangi, 27, of Erie, PA was sentenced to 16-36 months in state prison after pleading guilty to felony rioting and two misdemeanors for participation in the May 2020 Black Lives Matter protests in Erie. He is accused of throwing bricks at — and injuring — officers in the 500 block of State Street and smashing tables outside the Ember and Forge coffee shop.

Darion Lindsey, 19, was charged with arson after allegedly setting fire to a Chicago Transit Authority van during a 2020 protest in response to the death of George Floyd. Sentenced to 38 months federal prison.

On March 24, 2022 David Bermudez, 33, of Los Angeles, CA pled "no contest" to a charge of looting. Bermudez was arrested in Los Angeles by the Safe LA Task Force after the George Floyd Protests. Sentenced to 2 years in county jail.

Delveccho Waller Jr., 21, was indicted in Gainesville, GA with co-defendants Smallwood, Bailey, Thompson, and Martin for conspiring to commit and committing arson of a police car after a protest sparked by George Floyd's death in May 2020. Sentenced to 21 months federal prison plus 3 years supervised release and $3,678.17 restitution.

Denzal Stewart, 24, was charged with arson after allegedly setting fire to a Chicago Transit Authority van during a 2020 protest in response to the death of George Floyd. Sentenced to 45 months federal prison.

Surveillance video captured him piling trash against the sally-port door over 11 minutes, repeatedly lighting it and feeding the flames. While he was setting fires, others were attempting to disable the door with crowbars and cement-like materials. He was identified by his distinctive pink camouflage trousers. Sentenced to 20 months federal prison.

Devarian Haynes, 23, of Las Vegas was charged with co-defendants Tyree Walker and Ricardo Densmore for conspiracy to commit arson and arson after a May 30, 2020 video showed Walker and Haynes setting a police car on fire during protests over the death of George Floyd. Sentenced to 24 months federal prison.
Devon Vaughn, 23, was indicted on July 7, 2021 for setting fire to a furniture store at a Kenosha, WI protest in 2020. Sentenced to 40 months federal prison.

Sentenced to 30 months federal prison plus 3 years supervised release.

Edward Schinzing is a Portland, Oregon man who was sentenced to 15 months in federal prison for setting fire inside the Multnomah County Justice Center during the first night of George Floyd/BLM protests in Portland on May 29, 2020. He was identified from surveillance footage by a tattoo of his own last name across his back. He was indicted in August 2020 and pleaded guilty, receiving a significantly below-guidelines sentence reflecting a downward departure.

Edward Thomas Schinzing, 32, was charged July 28, 2020 with using fire to maliciously damage the Justice Center in downtown Portland on May 29, 2020. Identified by a distinctive last-name back tattoo. Pleaded guilty; 15 months federal prison + 3 years supervised release.
Edward William Carubis, 25, charged July 13, 2020 with assaulting federal officers in Portland by shining a green laser into three officers eyes. Pleaded guilty; 2 days time served.

Ellen Reiche is a Bellingham, Washington environmental and Indigenous solidarity activist convicted for placing a shunting device on BNSF railroad tracks near Bellingham, Washington on November 28, 2020. The device disrupted train signals at a moment when a crude oil tanker train was due through the area. Reiche was convicted by jury in September 2021 and sentenced to 12 months and one day in federal prison plus 3 years supervised release and 100 hours community service. She is a co-defendant with Samantha Brooks.

Ellen Brennan Reiche, age 28, of Bellingham WA, was indicted December 2020 under the federal anti-railroad-violence statute for placing a shunt on BNSF Railway tracks near Bellingham on November 28, 2020 in solidarity with the Wetsuweten pipeline-resistance struggle. Sentenced to 12 months and 1 day federal prison plus 3 years supervised release.

Emmanuel Quinones, 25, was arrested on May 30, 2020 in Lubbock, TX after brandishing a semi-automatic firearm at a Black Lives Matter protest at "low ready" position, causing the crowd to panic. He refused police commands to drop the rifle until officers drew their own guns and another protestor tackled him. He yelled statements like "This is a revolution" and "President Trump must die"; he admitted threatening Trump supporters and MAGA people on social media, claiming he would shoot them on sight. Sentenced to 46 months federal prison.

Errick Steven Toa, 33, jumped on top of an occupied police car and broke its windshield during the May 30, 2020 Fargo ND BLM protest. Charged July 15, 2020. Pleaded guilty; ~10.6 months time served + 2 years supervised release + $390 restitution.

Molotov arson of Dakota County government building (2020). Sentence: 78 months federal prison. Verified via public court/press records: https://www.justice.gov/usao-mn/pr/savage-man-sentenced-more-6-years-prison-arson-dakota-county-government-building

Fornandous Cortez Henderson, 32, was charged with arson and possession of a Molotov cocktail after setting fire to the Dakota County Western Service Center in Apple Valley, MN on May 29, 2020 — a government building housing state and local agencies and a U.S. Passport center. On March 24, 2022 Gabriela Brigitte Jimenez, 33, of Los Angeles, CA pled "no contest" to a charge of looting. She was arrested in Los Angeles by the "Safe LA Task Force" after the George Floyd Protests. Sentenced to 1 day in county jail.

Galen Sol Shireman-Grabowski, age 24, locked himself to a helicopter used by Mountain Valley Pipeline crews in Ellison, Virginia in October 2019, damaging the helicopter. Charged with multiple felonies and misdemeanors; pleaded guilty to four counts and received a 12-month suspended sentence plus $14,030.41 in restitution.

Molotov cocktails into Dakota County courthouse, Apple Valley (May 2020). Sentence: 60 months federal prison. Verified via public court/press records: https://patch.com/minnesota/applevalley-rosemount/man-sentenced-molotov-cocktail-attack-apple-valley-wsc-doj

Garrett Patrick Ziegler, 24, of Apple Valley, MN was charged with arson and possession of a Molotov cocktail with co-defendant Fornandous Cortez Henderson for the May 29, 2020 fire at the Dakota County Western Service Center. Sentenced to 60 months federal prison plus 3 years supervised release and $205,872.53 restitution.

George Allen, 31, of Pittsburgh, charged July 22, 2020 with civil disorder for damaging an occupied police vehicle by throwing an object through the front passenger window during the May 30, 2020 Pittsburgh BLM protest. Pleaded guilty; 12 months federal prison + 3 years supervised release.

Raekwon Dac Blankenship, 24, of Pittsburgh, charged July 22, 2020 with damaging unmarked and marked police vehicles by hitting/kicking/stomping and throwing a projectile through a windshield during the May 30, 2020 Pittsburgh BLM protest; also struck multiple police horses. Pleaded guilty; ~5.3 months (time served + 3 years supervised release).

Hampton Milton McCoy III, 29, of Tampa, FL was charged following his involvement in a Black Lives Matter protest over Memorial Day weekend 2020 — initially with burglary of an unoccupied structure and grand theft after allegedly breaking into a Gold and Diamond Source store. He pled no contest to burglary in exchange for the grand theft charge being dropped. Sentenced to 180 days in Florida state prison plus 24 months probation and 50 hours community service.

Henry Parker, 30, of Wichita, KS was sentenced to 25 years in prison for firing multiple gunshots at police officers during a June 2, 2020 protest in north Wichita following the death of George Floyd. To disperse the crowd, SWAT officers fired tear gas; Parker fired on the officers, striking 1-2 officers' riot helmets. He was found guilty July 22, 2022 and sentenced in March 2023. According to court records, Parker "was upset when a woman he called his sister was hit with a rubber bullet while she held a baby."
Henry Trigos-Celon, age 43, ELN member; detained in September 2020. Pleaded guilty in U.S. federal court to the ELN cocaine-trafficking conspiracy.
Jose Gabriel Alvarez-Ortiz, age 26, ELN member; detained in late 2020. Extradited and prosecuted in the Southern District of New York for the ELN cocaine-trafficking conspiracy.

Yamit Picon-Rodriguez, age 36, ELN member; detained in September 2020 in connection with a 20-year ELN cocaine-trafficking conspiracy from Colombia to the United States. Extradited and prosecuted in the Southern District of New York.

On June 30, 2020 Isaiah Bryant, 24, was arrested in Los Angeles, CA by the "Safe LA Task Force" after the George Floyd Protests. He was found guilty of looting; sentenced to 5 months county jail. Currently held at the 77th Division Jail on other charges.

Isaiah Lindsey-Salinas, 23, of Eugene, OR was indicted on charges of rioting, burglary, and theft after being arrested in connection with a May 2020 George Floyd protest in Eugene that turned violent — people damaging property, robbing businesses, and setting a fire in the middle of an intersection. Felony charges dropped; found guilty of misdemeanors. Sentenced to about 5 days in Oregon state prison.

Isaiah Willoughby is a Tacoma, Washington man who was sentenced to 24 months in federal prison for setting fire to the Seattle Police East Precinct during the CHOP/CHAZ (Capitol Hill Occupied Protest) autonomous zone. In the early morning of June 12, 2020, Willoughby poured gasoline and ignited a debris pile against the precinct wall and subsequently deleted social media posts to conceal his involvement. The East Precinct was the symbolic center of the CHOP zone, a multi-week occupation of several city blocks following the police killing of George Floyd. Willoughby pleaded guilty to federal arson and was sentenced in October 2021. After his release he ran as a candidate for Seattle City Council.

Isaiah Thomas Willoughby, 35, of Seattle, WA was arrested on a federal arson charge after his family recognized him by his distinctive yellow hoodie in surveillance video. He was seen on June 12, 2020 starting a small fire at the Seattle PD East Precinct, then within the protester-occupied zone on Capitol Hill (CHAZ/CHOP). Sentenced to 24 months federal prison.

On June 10, 2020 in Jacksonville, FL, Ivan Jacob Zecher, 27, was charged with felon in possession of a firearm and unlawful possession of an unregistered firearm. During a protest, a group blocking traffic was reportedly throwing rocks and water bottles at officers. Officers arrested Zecher; his backpack was leaking — they found a liquor bottle full of gasoline, a lighter, balloons full of liquid, and a hatchet. Case dropped (illegal arrest).

Jabari Devon Davis, 21, of Raleigh, NC was charged with attempting to damage by fire a vehicle owned by an institution receiving federal financial assistance and for attempting to set fire to a marked police vehicle in Raleigh after a demonstration over George Floyd's death. Caused ~$5,000 in damage. Arrested by ATF special agents on June 4, 2020. Sentenced to 30 months federal prison.

Federal civil disorder; role in burning a Salt Lake City police car (2020). Sentence: 24 months federal prison. Verified via public court/press records: https://www.justice.gov/usao-ut/pr/patton-sentenced-24-months-federal-prison-role-may-2020-salt-lake-city-civil-unrest

Jackson Stuart Tamowski Patton, 26, of Salt Lake City, UT was charged with one count of arson in interstate commerce for setting fire to a Salt Lake City PD vehicle during May 30, 2020 protests. Sentenced to 24 months federal prison plus 3 years supervised release and $2,500 restitution.

Jacob D. Little, 24, was charged September 10, 2020 with possession of a stolen firearm after stealing a Colt M4 rifle with suppressor from a Seattle PD photo-unit patrol vehicle abandoned during the May 30, 2020 Seattle BLM protest. Pleaded guilty; 16 months federal prison + 3 years supervised release + $4,446.12 restitution.

Javon Hardy, 24, set fire to a 32-by-8-foot mobile office at the Rochester Public Safety Building during the May 30, 2020 BLM protest, captured on Facebook Live yelling Let that bitch burn. Charged December 15, 2020. Pleaded guilty; 12 months federal prison + $14,504 restitution.

In June 2020 in Cleveland, OH, Jaywuan Peavy, 19, was charged with using a facility of interstate commerce to organize, promote, encourage, participate in, or carry on a riot after posting numerous calls to riot on Facebook. Case dismissed.

Jeffrey Richard Singer, 33, charged October 20, 2020 with civil disorder (charging at and shoulder-slamming officers in front of Portland City Hall on October 4, 2020) and theft of government property (stealing the US flag from the Gus Solomon Courthouse flagpole September 19, 2020). Pleaded guilty; 6 months federal prison.

On June 26, 2020 Jeremy J. Ryan, 31, of Madison, WI was charged with making terrorist threats and stalking (both felonies) plus other misdemeanors for allegedly threatening to release personal information about Dane County Sheriff Dave Mahoney and his family and calling on protestors to harass Mahoney's family home. Sentenced to 3 months in Wisconsin state prison.

On July 17, 2020 Jeremy Trapp, 24, was observed by an informant and NYPD officers attempting to cut the brake line of an NYPD van. He had been communicating with an undercover informant about wanting to cut brake lines on police vehicles, and participated in reconnaissance for a bridge he expressed wanting to set on fire — saying current protests weren't violent enough. He stated he wanted to harm police officers and supporters because they were racist and wanted to burn the bridge so that "white supremacists could not use it to get to Brooklyn from Staten Island." Sentenced to 18 months federal prison.

Jerritt Jeremy Pace is a Washington, DC man sentenced to three years in federal prison for attempting to burn a Metropolitan Police Department precinct station during BLM protests on May 29, 2020. Pace attempted to ignite a gasoline-filled detergent container outside the 4th District station after posting on Facebook, "I WILL BURN A [4th district] STATION DOWN" and "BURN IT DOWN" along with a map link to the station. He was held without bond throughout the case; a judge's opinion denying his release cited his "escalating violence" and the fact that he was on supervision for other matters when he committed the offense. He pleaded guilty via superseding information and was sentenced in June 2021.

In 2020 in Washington, DC, Jerritt Jeremy Pace, 39, was charged with receiving an explosive in interstate commerce, willfully threatening to damage a building by fire, and attempted arson. Pace announced on Facebook his intent to burn down a police station: "I WILL BURN A 12 STATION DOWN SO QUICK IF THIS COMES TO MY TOWN....PLEASE COME ON DC AND LETS RIOT." He filled a plastic laundry detergent container with gasoline and a wick and ignited it in front of the Fourth District Station; no damage to the building, but the container exploded and burned on the sidewalk. Pleaded guilty to one count of unlawful firearm manufacture; sentenced to time served plus 3 years supervised release.

Federal arson of a Gainesville GA police car (June 2020). Sentence: 21 months federal prison. Verified via public court/press records: https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndga/pr/gainesville-men-sentenced-federal-arson-charges-setting-fire-police-car-parked-officer

Jesse James Smallwood, 21, was indicted in Gainesville, GA in June 2020 with co-defendants Delveccho Waller Jr., Bruce Thompson, Judah Coleman Bailey, and Dashun Martin for conspiring to commit and committing arson of a police car after a protest sparked by George Floyd's death. The defendants allegedly sought out and burned the police vehicle using the protests as cover. Sentenced to 21 months federal prison plus 3 years supervised release and $3,678.17 restitution.

Jhajuan Sabb, 20, of Troy NY, made several Facebook Live videos threatening to throw bricks at the Troy PD, Troy police vehicles, and Troy City Hall during the June 2020 BLM protests, and offered instructions for making firebombs. Pleaded guilty; 8 months federal prison + 3 years supervised release.

During 2020 protests in Rochester, NY over the killing of Daniel Prude, John Michael Santiago, 24, threw fireworks at police officers and participated in blockading. Jordan Coyne, 25, threw rocks, bricks, pieces of concrete, and a tear gas canister at police officers and a police vehicle during the May 30, 2020 Pittsburgh protests after the murder of George Floyd. The tear gas canister struck an officer in the hand. Pleaded guilty; 18 months federal prison.

Joseph Ybarra is a 21-year-old who was sentenced to time served after roughly 18 months in federal pretrial detention for throwing an incendiary device at the Mark O. Hatfield U.S. Courthouse in Portland, Oregon during protests on July 22, 2020. Ybarra had arrived in Portland by bus from Seattle the day before, originally intending to turn himself in on an unrelated Multnomah County warrant, and became swept up in the protest. Judah Coleman Bailey, 20, was indicted in Gainesville, GA with co-defendants Smallwood, Waller, Thompson, and Martin for conspiring to commit and committing arson of a police car after a protest sparked by George Floyd's death in May 2020. Sentenced to 21 months federal prison plus 3 years supervised release and $3,678.17 restitution.

About the Case

Kevin Olliff (aka Kevin Johnson) and Tyler Lang were indicted under the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act for allegedly releasing—and conspiring to release—about 2,000 mink and foxes from Midwest fur farms. They were arrested during the summer of 2013 and took non-cooperating plea deals on state charges of “possession of burglary tools.” Then almost a year later, they were indicted on federal AETA charges. During the summer of 2015, Kevin and Tyler entered into a non-cooperating plea agreements through which they plead guilty to violating the AETA.

Although it may seem ridiculous to charge people with “terrorism” for allegedly saving animals from living in barren wire cages and being killed by methods that may include anal electrocution or having their necks snapped, the ridiculousness speaks to what is beneath the surface of this legislation. The AETA was crafted by the American Legislative Exchange Council, a group of corporate power players who write pieces of model legislation that suit their interests, and then ALEC passes off the legislation to members of Congress. Many members of ALEC are part of the pharmaceutical, big ag, and other industries that exploit and kill animals for profit—industries that have a huge interest in stopping the actions of animal liberation activists.

To add to the mix, the State uses the label of “terrorism” with a lot of flexibility in order to be able to manipulate public fear based on the State interests of the day, and this context left the label open for ALEC to apply it to animal liberation activists. And so ALEC devised the AETA, legislation not meant so much for prosecuting activists (Kevin and Tyler are among only a handful of people who’ve been charged under the AETA), but to conjure public fear of the animal liberation movement and deter people from getting involved in activism, let alone from freeing animals from the hell of fur farms.

In the early hours of July 28, 2012 — the day before the Hiroshima anniversary — she, Vietnam veteran Michael Walli (then 63), and former U.S. Army officer Greg Boertje-Obed (then 57), all three Catholic peace activists, cut through three perimeter fences and walked into the Y-12 National Security Complex at Oak Ridge, Tennessee. al-Amin spoke at a Civil Rights Movement rally in Cambridge, Maryland on July 24, 1967 (during the "Long Hot Summer of 1967"). A fire started that night expanded across city blocks and al-Amin was charged with inciting a riot, due to his speech. However, a secret 1967 FBI memo had called for "neutralizing" Brown; and historian Dr. Peter Levy found that there was no riot, al-Amin was shot by a police officer without provocation, and the fire was unrelated, having spread so drastically because the city's fire department refused to respond to the predominantly Black neighborhood. After the attempt on his life, al-Amin disappeared for 18 months. 

In a October 1971 standoff with police, he was shot and seized, and spent five years in Attica prison. From 1992 to 1997, the FBI closely surveilled al-Amin, generating pages of 44,000 documents. In 2000, two sheriffs came to al-Amin’s store with a warrant for failure to appear in court for a case later thrown out. Both were shot and one killed. al-Amin was sentenced to life without parole, even though Otis Jackson confessed to the shootings. al-Amin has filed for multiple appeals, only for them to be denied despite his old age, blindness and cancer diagnosis.

(1969), and one of the most prominent Black Power figures of the late 1960s. After his prison conversion to Sunni Islam he became the imam of the Atlanta Community Mosque and a leading figure in the Imam Jamil Action Network and Dar ul-Islam mosque movement. The Atlanta community mosque he led at the West End drew thousands and was widely credited with reducing drug-related crime in the neighborhood.

On March 16, 2000, Fulton County Sheriffs Deputies Ricky Kinchen and Aldranon English approached him outside his West End store to execute a warrant. Gunfire was exchanged; Kinchen was killed and English was wounded. He fled and was apprehended four days later in White Hall, Alabama. On March 9, 2002 he was convicted by a Fulton County jury and on March 14, 2002 sentenced to life without the possibility of parole.

His defense and supporters consistently maintained that the conviction relied on disputed eyewitness identifications and that another man — federal inmate Otis Jackson — had repeatedly confessed under oath to having committed the killings. The Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Imam Jamil Action Network, and other Muslim civil rights organizations called for the case to be reopened. He died at FMC Butner in North Carolina on November 23, 2025, age 82, while still serving the life sentence.
