In the early hours of November 2, 2009, Bix — then 81 years old — and four other Catholic activists (including the late Anne Montgomery RSCJ, Susan Crane, Steve Kelly SJ, and Lynne Greenwald) cut through three security fences and entered the Strategic Weapons Facility Pacific at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor, where the U.S. Pacific fleet's Trident D-5 nuclear warheads are stored. They reached the inner perimeter, where they hung banners, scattered sunflower seeds, and waited to be arrested. The action became known as the Disarm Now Plowshares. The five were charged with conspiracy, trespass, destruction of property, and depredation of government property. After a December 2010 trial they were convicted by a federal jury in Tacoma. Bix was sentenced in March 2011 to three months in federal prison plus four months of home confinement.

In 2010 he had also served three months at FCI Marianna for an SOA Watch border crossing at Fort Benning. He died on February 28, 2015 at age 86. Father Bill 'Bix' Bichsel SJ was an American Jesuit priest, peace activist with the Ground Zero Center for Nonviolent Action in Poulsbo, Washington, and one of the most consistently arrested U.S. anti-nuclear and SOA Watch activists. He was sentenced to twelve months in federal prison in connection with the September 29, 1997 SOA sign-altering action at Fort Benning. He served at FPC Sheridan, Oregon. Bichsel later participated in the November 2, 2009 Disarm Now Plowshares action at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor and died in 2015.

On September 29, 1997, five activists — Father Bill Bichsel SJ, Sister Marge Eilerman OSF, Ed Kinane, Mary Trotochaud, and others — altered the entrance sign at the U.S. Army School of the Americas at Fort Benning, Georgia. The five were tried in October 1998 in federal court in Columbus, GA and sentenced to 8 to 12 months in federal prison. Held at Federal Prison Camp Sheridan, Oregon (Unit 5, BOP register 86275-020) for participating in the School of the Americas Watch annual line-crossing protest at Fort Benning, GA.

Edward Zabo, age 49, was a co-conspirator with John Ford and Joseph Mazzuchelli in the 1996 Long Island UFO Network plot to use radium against Suffolk County officials. Pleaded guilty to supplying radioactive materials; 12 months state prison.

Gazi Ibrahim Abu Mezer, 25, Palestinian foreign national, was indicted August 28, 1997 for plotting to detonate pipe bombs in the NYC subway in an attempted suicide attack to kill as many Jews as possible in protest of the Israeli/Palestinian conflict. Convicted; life without parole.

John J. Ford, age 47, was president of the Long Island UFO Network. He and two co-conspirators were arrested in June 1996 over a plot to use radium-laced canisters to murder Suffolk County Republican leader John Powell and two county officials, accusing the local government of covering up UFO sightings. Found incompetent to stand trial.

Joseph Mazzuchelli, age 42, was a co-conspirator with John Ford and Edward Zabo in a 1996 plot to use radium-laced canisters to murder Suffolk County Republican leader John Powell and two county officials. Pleaded guilty to second-degree conspiracy and related charges; 36 months state prison.

Lafi Khalil, 25, foreign national, was indicted August 28, 1997 with co-defendant Gazi Ibrahim Abu Mezer for a plot to detonate pipe bombs in the NYC subway during rush hour. Acquitted on conspiracy/WMD count; convicted on immigration-related charges. 36 months federal prison.

Jason Troff, age 19, was one of four animal-rights activists who set fire to a McDonalds under construction in West Jordan, Utah in 1996, destroying about 80 percent of the building. Sentenced to 12 months federal prison.
Mark Klein, age 19, was one of four animal-rights activists who set fire to a McDonalds under construction in West Jordan, Utah in 1996. Sentenced to 12 months federal prison.

Ryan Durfee, age 19, was one of four animal-rights activists who set fire to a McDonalds under construction in West Jordan, Utah in 1996. Sentenced to 12 months federal prison plus 200 hours community service.

Tsutomu Shirosaki was a member of the Japanese Red Army convicted in U.S. federal court in 1998 over the 1986 rocket attack on the U.S. embassy in Jakarta, and sentenced to 30 years. Released for good behavior in January 2015, he was deported to Japan, where he was tried and imprisoned again. He died at Fuchu Prison in Tokyo on July 20, 2024, at age 76.

Charles Damien Darden, 17, drove the car in the January 14, 1995 Westerman shooting (Morrow shot from passenger seat). Convicted of first-degree murder, civil rights intimidation, and attempted aggravated kidnapping. Life sentence plus 3+4 years concurrent with each other but consecutive to life.

Freddie Morrow, 17, with co-defendants Damien Darden, Marcus Merriweather, and Tony Andrews, followed and shot Michael Westerman near Guthrie KY on January 14, 1995 after seeing a Confederate flag flying from his pickup. Westerman died. Morrow pulled the trigger. Convicted of first-degree murder, civil-rights intimidation, and attempted aggravated kidnapping; sentenced to life plus consecutive 4 + 5 = 9 years.

Frederick Urban, age 46, was arrested April 1995 in Scranton, Pennsylvania while driving a van containing explosive devices; statements he made indicated intent to use the explosives against the federal government and a right-wing anti-government ideology. Convicted at trial of possession of an unregistered destructive device with a special-skill enhancement.

Jamie L. Boulter, age 18, was charged in 1995 with aggravated arson for allegedly throwing a Molotov cocktail into the Majestic Meats meatpacking plant in Salt Lake City, Utah. Charges were ultimately dismissed.
Marcus Merriweather, 15, passenger in the January 14, 1995 Westerman shooting car. Found not guilty on all charges.
Tony Andrews, 17, passenger in the January 14, 1995 Westerman shooting car. Pleaded guilty and testified against co-defendants in return for 24 months probation.

Katherine Ann Power was a 21-year-old Brandeis University student and Susan Saxes co-defendant in the September 1970 Brighton MA bank robbery and the September 1970 Newburyport armory raid. She went underground immediately after the robbery and lived as Alice Louise Metzinger in Lebanon, Oregon for the next 23 years — building a life as a restaurant owner, mother, and activist before she negotiated a surrender on September 15, 1993. She pleaded guilty to manslaughter and armed robbery and was sentenced to 8 to 12 years in Massachusetts state prison; she was paroled on October 6, 1999 after 6 years.

Artur Tchibassa, 47, FLEC member, was indicted September 25, 1991 in DC for the kidnapping of a Chevron employee in Angola; acted as negotiator/spokesperson for the kidnappers. Pleaded guilty; 293 months federal prison.
Anthony Smyth, 43, US citizen, IRA gun-running co-defendant; convicted; 36 months federal prison.

Conor Claxton, 27, Irish foreign national, was indicted July 26, 1999 in Florida along with co-defendants Anthony Smyth, Martin Mullen, and Siobhan Browne for IRA gun-running: purchasing weapons and ammunition in Florida and mailing them to Northern Ireland. Convicted; 56 months federal prison.
Martin Mullen, 30, Irish foreign national, IRA gun-running co-defendant; convicted; 36 months federal prison.

Siobhan Browne, 37, US citizen, was charged July 26, 1999 with conspiracy to mail weapons and Arms Export Control Act violations after buying 27 guns in Florida to support the IRA. Pleaded guilty; 20 months federal prison.

Samuel Sánchez, a 28-year-old mental-health worker, was held in civil contempt on January 24, 1989 by Judge Eugene Nickerson for refusing to cooperate with a Brooklyn federal grand jury investigating the FALN / Puerto Rican independence movement. He had been subpoenaed days after undergoing skull-reconstruction surgery; FBI agents reportedly tried to interrogate him at his hospital bedside. He refused to inform, telling the court, "I say no to the grand jury."

Father Jerome 'Jerry' Zawada OFM was a Franciscan friar of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary Province (later the Sacred Heart Province) and a peace activist whose six decades of ministry included extensive work in the Philippines, in Nicaragua during the Contra war, and at U.S. military installations. He was arrested dozens of times across his life, primarily for SOA Watch line-crossings at Fort Benning, Georgia, and for protests at the Nevada Test Site, serving multiple short federal sentences. He died in 2017 at age 80.

Convicted in U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Georgia under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) for participating in the School of the Americas Watch (SOA Watch) annual nonviolent civil-disobedience action at Fort Benning, Georgia on September 2002. The action targeted the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Institute for Security Cooperation (WHINSEC) — formerly the School of the Americas — which had trained Latin American military officers later linked to assassinations, torture, and massacres including Romero, the four U.S. churchwomen, the Jesuits in El Salvador, El Mozote, and Plan Cóndor. Defendants typically received 3 to 6 months in federal custody plus a fine.

Andrew Lawrence was a 28-year-old former Peace Corps volunteer and peace activist living at Jonah House in Baltimore, also described as associated with the Community for Creative Non-Violence. On Easter Sunday, April 3, 1988, he joined Philip Berrigan, Sister Margaret McKenna and Gregory Boertje in boarding the USS Iowa with a public tour at Norfolk Naval Station. Calling themselves the Nuclear Navy Plowshares, the four separated from the tour, used hammers and bolt cutters against two armored Tomahawk cruise-missile launcher boxes, poured blood on the equipment and displayed banners reading “Seek the Disarmed Christ” and “Tomahawks Into Plowshares,” stopping when naval security ordered them to. Lawrence was arrested and charged with federal criminal trespass. Although offered release on personal recognizance, he refused and remained jailed in solidarity with Boertje, whose bond had been set at $25,000 over an earlier Plowshares prosecution. Tried without a jury before U.S. Magistrate Tommy Miller, Lawrence admitted the action but argued it was justified by international law and the threat posed by nuclear weapons; he was convicted on May 19, 1988 and sentenced on July 21, 1988 to four months in prison, having by then already spent 109 days in custody. He was then transferred to a Philadelphia jail to face a separate charge connected with hanging a banner from the federal courthouse roof during one of the Epiphany Plowshares trials; his final release date has not been recovered.

An Oblate priest and longtime anti-nuclear resister, Kabat is best known for the 1984 “Silo Pruning Hooks” action in which four activists cut through fencing at a Minuteman II missile silo site in Missouri, damaged the silo’s concrete lid with tools, and conducted prayers as a direct challenge to nuclear weapons policy.

Arrested at the site, he was convicted in federal court (including conspiracy, trespass, and property-damage charges) and sentenced to ten years in prison—one of the longest sentences imposed on anti-nuclear civil disobedience from that period. Father Paul Kabat was an Oblate Catholic priest and the older brother of Plowshares activist Father Carl Kabat. On November 12, 1984 he joined his brother, Helen Woodson, and Larry Cloud Morgan in the Silo Pruning Hooks action at a Minuteman II missile silo near Knob Noster, Missouri. He was sentenced to 8 years in federal prison; he served until 1989. He died on June 22, 2007, age 72.

Catholic priest of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate (OMI) and brother of Carl Kabat, participant in the Silo Pruning Hooks Plowshares action on November 12, 1984 at a Minuteman II silo in Missouri. Convicted of sabotage and depredation of government property and sentenced to federal prison alongside his brother, Larry Cloud-Morgan, and Helen Woodson. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

Sister Darlene Nicgorski was a School Sister of St. Francis who became a leading organizer of the Sanctuary Movement after the 1980 murder of a priest she had worked with in Guatemala convinced her of the dangers facing the people she helped. A central defendant in the 1985–86 Tucson sanctuary trial — singled out, her supporters charged, for especially aggressive treatment by the prosecution — she was arrested after a search of her home in January 1985 and convicted on May 1, 1986 of conspiracy and alien-smuggling charges for her work aiding Central American refugees. Like her co-defendants, she was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Earl H. Carroll to probation rather than prison. Nicgorski remained an outspoken advocate for refugees and a critic of U.S. policy in Central America.

Born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, Nicgorski entered the School Sisters of St. Francis in 1966 and made final profession in 1974. After her Franciscan mentor Father Tulio Maruzzo was assassinated in Guatemala in July 1981, she came to Arizona to coordinate the national Sanctuary Movement's referral network for Guatemalan and Salvadoran refugees from Phoenix. She was the most prominent Catholic woman religious in the prosecution. She left the SSSF in 1987 and worked the rest of her life as a peace and women's-rights activist; her papers are at the Claremont Colleges Library. She died Feb 28, 2017 in Pomona, California, aged 73.

Yvette Kelly was a Black liberation activist charged as a New York 8+ defendant in the October 1984 federal RICO indictment alleging a conspiracy to free Sundiata Acoli, commit armed bank expropriations, and bomb federal buildings. She was arrested on October 18, 1984, when 400 FBI agents staged pre-dawn raids just three days after the new federal preventive-detention law took effect — prosecutors immediately sought to hold the defendants without bail on the political nature of the charges, making the case an early test of the 1984 Bail Reform Act. In August 1985 the jury acquitted the New York 8 of all RICO and conspiracy counts. Friends and family of the defendants, including a 15-year-old, were subpoenaed to a grand jury and refused to collaborate.

Agnes Gertrude Bauerlein was a Dutch-born mother, grandmother, and lifelong social activist in Ambler and Philadelphia. Having lost a brother and sister in WWII bombings of the Netherlands, she devoted her life to peace work; she and her husband opened their Ambler home to the Plowshares Eight defendants during the 1981 Norristown trial, traveled to Iraq with the Gulf Peace Team in 1991 to try to avert war, and was repeatedly jailed for nonviolent action. She died at age 87 of complications from Alzheimer's, survived by 11 children, 26 grandchildren, and 13 great-grandchildren.

Macy Morse was a mother and grandmother from Nashua, NH whose three oldest sons served in the military, one in Vietnam, prompting her conversion to active pacifism. She co-founded the Nashua, NH People Concerned About the War in Vietnam and accumulated more than 60 years of nonviolent activism, at least 10 arrests, and four jail terms — including for splashing blood in Alexander Haig's office in 1981 and for trespassing in Sen. Judd Gregg's office in 2003. She died at age 98.

Vern Rossman was an ordained minister of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), born Feb. 3, 1927, raised in a minister's family in Oklahoma, educated at Phillips University and Yale Divinity School (ordained 1951). He served as a missionary to Japan from 1952 to 1963, where the legacy of Hiroshima and Nagasaki shaped his lifelong commitment to peace and anti-nuclear work; he later worked for the Disciples' Division of Overseas Ministries in Indianapolis and as executive director of Intermedia in NYC under the World Council of Churches. At the time of Griffiss he was a 56-year-old father and grandfather living in Dorchester, MA. He died at his home in Columbia, Missouri in 2014.

Plowshares peace activist arrested in a disarmament action against nuclear weapons systems in the 1980s. Convicted of federal sabotage and depredation of government property. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

Father Louis Vitale OFM was an American Franciscan friar, U.S. Air Force veteran (he served as a pilot before entering religious life), and one of the most prolific civil-disobedience peace activists in modern U.S. history — arrested more than 200 times across five decades. He co-founded the Nevada Desert Experience in 1982, the long-running organizing campaign against U.S. nuclear testing at the Nevada Test Site, and Pace e Bene Nonviolence Service in 1989. He served as Pastor of St. Boniface Church in San Francisco's Tenderloin neighborhood from 1992 to 2005, where he ran the largest meal program for unhoused people in the city.

Most of his arrests were short Nevada Test Site trespasses, but he served substantial federal time for two later actions. On November 19, 2006, with Father Steve Kelly SJ, he crossed the line at Fort Huachuca, Arizona — the U.S. Army's interrogation school where post-9/11 'enhanced interrogation' techniques were taught — and attempted to deliver a letter to the commanding general protesting U.S. torture policy. They were convicted of trespass and sentenced to five months federal in May 2007; both were 75 years old at the time. In 2007 he was also sentenced to five months for the annual SOA Watch line-crossing at Fort Benning, Georgia, served at FCI Lompoc. He died on June 21, 2023 at age 91. Convicted in U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Georgia under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) for participating in the School of the Americas Watch (SOA Watch) annual nonviolent civil-disobedience action at Fort Benning, Georgia on September 2002. The action targeted the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Institute for Security Cooperation (WHINSEC) — formerly the School of the Americas — which had trained Latin American military officers later linked to assassinations, torture, and massacres including Romero, the four U.S. churchwomen, the Jesuits in El Salvador, El Mozote, and Plan Cóndor. Defendants typically received 3 to 6 months in federal custody plus a fine.

Benjamin H. Sasway was the first American indicted since the Vietnam War for refusing to register with the Selective Service System, and the first jailed for it. A 21-year-old San Diego State University student, Sasway had refused to register in 1980 and said openly and often that draft registration was "immoral and incompatible with a free society." Indicted in San Diego in 1982, he was barred at trial from telling the jury about his political motives, and in August 1982 a federal jury — after deliberating about 50 minutes — convicted him of refusing to register. On October 4, 1982 a judge sentenced him to 30 months in a minimum-security federal prison, making him the first person imprisoned for draft-registration resistance since the Vietnam era.

Political-science and philosophy student at Humboldt State who became the first man indicted for failure to register since the Vietnam War. Selected for the test prosecution at the recommendation of Reagan adviser Edwin Meese, who believed conservative San Diego would deliver a quick conviction. Indicted June 30, 1982; convicted by a jury after only 40 minutes' deliberation on Aug. 26, 1982; sentenced Oct. 4, 1982 to 30 months in federal prison — the harshest sentence of any nonregistrant. Barred from telling the jury his motives. Served until release on Sept. 20, 1985.

Provisional IRA volunteer born January 20, 1955 in the New Lodge area of Belfast. Interned without charge at age 17 in 1972 under British internment. Arrested in 1980 with his IRA Active Service Unit after an ambush in which British Captain Herbert Westmacott was killed; escaped from Crumlin Road Jail during his 1981 trial. Came to the U.S. and was arrested by federal officials in New York on June 18, 1983 on immigration charges. Held at MCC New York for over five years while the U.S. fought to extradite him; in 1984 a federal judge ruled the IRA ambush was a political offense barring extradition. Spent over nine years in U.S. federal custody (mostly MCC and Otisville) before being deported back to Northern Ireland in February 1992. Released under the Good Friday Agreement in 1998.

Sister Anne Montgomery, RSCJ, of the Society of the Sacred Heart was one of the most prolific Plowshares activists in U.S. history, participating in seven Plowshares actions over thirty years and serving roughly six years of cumulative federal prison time. She was one of the original Plowshares Eight at the King of Prussia GE plant in 1980, then participated in Trident Plowshares (1982), Pershing Plowshares (1984), Riverside Plowshares (1992), Aegis Plowshares (1995), Trident II Plowshares (1995), and finally — at age 83 — the Disarm Now Plowshares action at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor on November 2, 2009 alongside Bill 'Bix' Bichsel SJ, Steve Kelly SJ, Susan Crane, and Lynne Greenwald. Convicted in the Disarm Now case at age 84, she received a sentence of two months plus four months of home confinement. She died in 2012 at age 85.

On September 9, 1980, eight Catholic peace activists — Daniel Berrigan, Philip Berrigan, Carl Kabat, Anne Montgomery RSCJ, Molly Rush, Elmer Maas, John Schuchardt, and Dean Hammer — entered the General Electric Re-entry Systems Division plant in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, where Mark 12A nuclear warhead nose cones were manufactured. They hammered on two of the nose cones and poured their own blood on documents, in a literal enactment of the prophet Isaiah's image of beating swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4). They were arrested at the scene and went to trial in Norristown the following year. Convicted of burglary, conspiracy, and criminal mischief, they were sentenced in 1981 to terms of 3 to 10 years; the case was on appeal for ten years before they were resentenced in 1990 to time served (just over a year). The action launched the modern Plowshares movement, which has carried out more than 100 symbolic disarmament actions worldwide since.

Elmer Maas was a musician, music teacher, and Catholic peace activist who joined the Plowshares Eight at the GE plant in King of Prussia in September 1980 and remained part of the Plowshares movement for the rest of his life, participating in additional actions and supporting prisoners of conscience. He died in December 2002 at age 67.

On September 9, 1980, eight Catholic peace activists — Daniel Berrigan, Philip Berrigan, Carl Kabat, Anne Montgomery RSCJ, Molly Rush, Elmer Maas, John Schuchardt, and Dean Hammer — entered the General Electric Re-entry Systems Division plant in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, where Mark 12A nuclear warhead nose cones were manufactured. They hammered on two of the nose cones and poured their own blood on documents, in a literal enactment of the prophet Isaiah's image of beating swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4). They were arrested at the scene and went to trial in Norristown the following year. Convicted of burglary, conspiracy, and criminal mischief, they were sentenced in 1981 to terms of 3 to 10 years; the case was on appeal for ten years before they were resentenced in 1990 to time served (just over a year). The action launched the modern Plowshares movement, which has carried out more than 100 symbolic disarmament actions worldwide since.

Quaker organizer and longtime AFSC director of the Nonviolent Movement Building Program. Helped form both the Pledge of Resistance and the Nuremberg Action Group blockading Concord Naval Weapons Station. Arrested more than 150 times across his career, beginning with a 1960 lunch-counter sit-in. Co-founded Nonviolent Peaceforce (2002) and World Beyond War (2014). Died March 2025 at age 84 — final arrest weeks before his death at Travis Air Force Base.

A 30-year-old Black student in New York City accused of slashing an undercover 'decoy' policeman; The Black Panther Vol. 19 no.6 (1979) reports Judge Bruce Wright released him without bail given his lack of record and community ties, sparking a political controversy. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v19 no.6; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

William Phillips Africa is a member of MOVE, the Philadelphia-based Black liberation and back-to-nature group founded by John Africa, and one of the "MOVE 9." Following the August 8, 1978 armed police confrontation at MOVE's Powelton Village house — in which Officer James Ramp was killed — the nine surviving adult members were convicted of third-degree murder in 1980 and each sentenced to 30 to 100 years. He died in prison in 2015, still incarcerated after more than 36 years.

Phil Africa was a member of the MOVE organization arrested with eight other MOVE members in the August 8, 1978 Philadelphia police raid on the MOVE compound at 33rd and Powelton. He was convicted along with the rest of the MOVE 9 of third-degree murder of Officer James J. Ramp. He died in Pennsylvania state prison on January 10, 2015 at age 59 — the second of the MOVE 9 to die behind bars, after Merle Africas death in 1998.

Merle Austin Africa is documented as one of the MOVE 9, placing her activism within MOVE’s broader Philadelphia history of radical communal organizing and direct confrontation with city authority. In accounts of MOVE, the MOVE 9 convictions became a central, long-running focus of organizing by supporters, with imprisoned members—including Merle Africa—frequently cited in campaigns against perceived political repression and punitive policing.
She was arrested on Aug. 8, 1978 after the Powelton Village confrontation and was convicted of third-degree murder alongside the other MOVE 9, receiving a decades-long sentence. She died while incarcerated in 1998. Merle Africa was a member of the MOVE organization arrested with eight other MOVE members in the August 8, 1978 Philadelphia police raid on the MOVE compound at 33rd and Powelton. She was convicted along with the rest of the MOVE 9 of third-degree murder of Officer James J. Ramp. She died in Pennsylvania state prison in March 1998 at age 47 — the first of the MOVE 9 to die behind bars.

Tommy Lee Hines was a 25-year-old Black man with a severe intellectual disability — an IQ of about 39, described by doctors as having the mind of a young child — living in Decatur, Alabama, when in 1978 he was charged with the rape and robbery of three white women. Picked up for loitering on May 23, 1978, he was within hours accused of the three assaults; though illiterate, he was confronted with a written "confession" that was later used against him.

His prosecution became one of the most explosive civil-rights confrontations of the late 1970s. The Southern Christian Leadership Conference led large marches in Decatur and — after the trial was moved — in Cullman, met by Ku Klux Klan counter-demonstrations; during a 1979 Decatur march, gunfire wounded two Black marchers and two Klansmen. An all-white jury convicted Hines in October 1978 and he was sentenced to 30 years, and he was held at the Kilby Correctional Facility. In 1980 the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals reversed the conviction (Hines v. State); a court ordered a competency hearing, and Hines was committed to a state mental hospital rather than retried.

Elderly, blind, diabetic Black woman imprisoned in Wisconsin on perjury and welfare-fraud charges The Black Panther Vol. 17 no.15 (1977) calls a frame-up in retaliation for her testimony that she saw a white Milwaukee policeman shoot a 16-year-old Black youth (Jerry Brookshire) in the back in 1974; her home was firebombed twice. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v17 no.15; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Robert Eugene Robideau was an American Indian Movement organizer and a member of the AIM spiritual encampment at the Jumping Bull family compound on the Pine Ridge Reservation on June 26, 1975, when FBI agents Jack Coler and Ronald Williams entered the compound in unmarked cars looking for an alleged stolen-boots suspect and were killed in the firefight that followed. He, Darrelle Dean Butler, Leonard Peltier, and Jimmy Eagle were federally indicted for the agents murders. He was held in pretrial detention from his September 1975 arrest until his July 1976 acquittal at trial in U.S. District Court in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, where the jury accepted the defense argument that the defendants had fired in self-defense in the climate of the Pine Ridge reign of terror.

After his acquittal he became one of the principal organizers of the international Free Leonard Peltier campaign and a longtime spokesperson for AIM. He died on February 17, 2009 at age 62.

Safiya Bukhari, born Bernice Jones in The Bronx in 1950, was a member of the New York chapter of the Black Panther Party, a soldier in the Black Liberation Army, and the principal co-founder of the Jericho Movement for amnesty for U.S. political prisoners. She joined the BPP after witnessing New York police harass a Panther selling The Black Panther newspaper on a Harlem street. After the 1971 split that destroyed the BPP as a national organization she went underground with the Black Liberation Army.

She was arrested in Norfolk, Virginia in January 1975 in connection with a Black Liberation Army attempted robbery and convicted of armed robbery. She was sentenced to a long term in the Virginia state prison system, escaped briefly in 1976, and was recaptured. She served nine years, much of it at the Bedford Hills Correctional Facility for Women in New York after a transfer, before her release in 1983.

With Jalil Muntaqim and others, she founded the Jericho Movement in 1998 to demand the release of all U.S. political prisoners. She served as its first national chair until her death from a heart attack on August 24, 2003 at age 53. Her collected essays and speeches were published posthumously as The War Before (2010), with a foreword by her daughter Wonda Jones.

Antonio Quintana was a 22-year-old member of the Denver Chicano-movement organization Crusade for Justice. The Black Panther reported that he was arrested with Juan Haro on September 17, 1975 and falsely charged with conspiring to bomb several Denver police stations, in what the paper called a sensationalized set-up built on the testimony of the agent provocateur José Cordova Jr., timed to coincide with a national police-chiefs meeting in Denver. Their conspiracy trial was set to begin January 12, 1977.

A 25-year-old Black man arrested by Marshall County, Mississippi deputies on a 1975 armed-robbery charge who was found dead in his cell (hands and feet bound) on Jan. 21, 1978; officials ruled suicide, but the United League of Marshall County disputed it and demanded a federal probe. The Black Panther Vol. 18 no.7 (1978). [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v18 no.7; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Susan Edith Saxe was a 21-year-old Brandeis University student in 1970 and one of the principal organizers of a small anti-war affinity group that planned to fund underground militant action through bank robberies. On September 20, 1970 she and Katherine Ann Power were among five who carried out an armed raid on the Newburyport, Massachusetts National Guard armory; on September 23, 1970 they participated in an armed robbery of a State Street Bank branch in the Brighton neighborhood of Boston in which co-defendant William Gilday shot Boston Police Officer Walter Schroeder in the back as he responded to the call.

She went underground after the robbery and was placed on the FBI Most Wanted list on October 17, 1970 — one of the first U.S. women on the list. She was captured in Philadelphia on March 27, 1975 and was convicted of bank robbery, manslaughter, and conspiracy. She served five years in Massachusetts state prison; she was released in 1982. After her release she became a longtime Philadelphia Jewish-feminist organizer and the executive director of the Bread and Roses Community Fund.

Milton Eugene Lindsey was a 23-year-old Black worker, husband and father of two in Chattanooga, Tennessee. Early on July 21, 1974, police officers Paul O'Rear and Buddy Hullander entered a Black nightclub on Main Street without cause, demanded identification, and arrested him; one officer told the other, per Lindsey, to stop in an alley and beat him, which they did with pistols, blackjacks, boots and spit, leaving multiple lacerations to his head and back. Officers then charged him with public drunkenness and assault and battery on police officers. At trial the defense produced a Polaroid of an officer with a swollen eye alleging Lindsey had assaulted him, but witnesses — including the officers themselves — testified Lindsey was not drunk, was never given a drunk test, and was not staggering; the judge dismissed the drunkenness charge yet still handed down suspended sentences on two counts of assault and battery and a 92-dollar fine. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974).

Cal Ray Biggins was an 18-year-old Black Dallas youth indicted by the Dallas County grand jury for the January 7, 1974 murder of an elderly couple in their store. He was arrested four days later after a 5,000-dollar reward was offered and a paid informer called police to implicate him. The Black Panther reported the case as a frame-up; more than fifty supporters organized around his aunt, Mrs. Roberta King, with the Dallas Chapter of the Party. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, February 23, 1974; disposition not located.

Elliott White Haskins was a 25-year-old man alleged to be a member of the Black Liberation Army. He was wanted in Freeport, Long Island, on a murder charge dating to February 4, 1972 when, on October 3, 1973, he was among four men arrested with the BLA fugitive Henry "Sha Sha" Brown in a police raid on a tenement at 79 Menahan Street in the Bushwick section of Brooklyn. The Brooklyn District Attorney said the men taken with Brown would be charged with harboring him and hindering prosecution. The outcome of the charges against Haskins is not documented in the available sources.

Timothy Adams was a 25-year-old man from Bennettsville, South Carolina, alleged to be a member of the Black Liberation Army. He was already under indictment for the 1971 attempted murder of two Brooklyn police officers when, on October 3, 1973, he was one of four men arrested alongside the BLA fugitive Henry "Sha Sha" Brown in a police raid on a tenement at 79 Menahan Street in the Bushwick section of Brooklyn. The Brooklyn District Attorney announced that the men arrested with Brown would be charged with harboring him and hindering prosecution. The outcome of the charges against Adams is not documented in the available sources.

Veronza Leon Bowers Jr. was a member of the Kansas City chapter of the Black Panther Party. He was arrested in 1973 in connection with the June 1973 killing of U.S. National Park Service ranger Kenneth Patrick at Point Reyes National Seashore in California. The federal prosecution rested almost entirely on the testimony of two government informants who received reduced sentences on unrelated charges in exchange for their testimony. He was convicted in 1974 of first-degree murder of a federal officer and sentenced to life with the possibility of parole.

Under the federal sentencing structure in effect at the time of his conviction he became eligible for mandatory parole on April 7, 2004 after 30 years served. The U.S. Parole Commission has repeatedly denied his release in defiance of the mandatory-parole statute, drawing federal litigation across two decades. He was finally released from the Federal Medical Center in Butner, North Carolina on May 24, 2024 — age 78, after 51 years in federal prison and ranking as the longest-held federal political prisoner in U.S. history. The Jericho Movement and the Anarchist Black Cross Federation made his case a central campaign for decades.

Veronza was a member of the Black Panther Party who was convicted in the murder of a U.S. Park Ranger on the word of two government informants, both of whom received reduced sentences for other crimes by Federal prosecutors. There were no eye-witnesses and no evidence independent of the informants to link him to the crime. At trial, Veronza offered alibi testimony, not credited by the jury. Nor was testimony of two relatives of the informants who insisted that they were lying. The informants had all charges against them in this case dropped and one was given $10,000 by the government according to the prosecutor’s post-sentencing report. Veronza has consistently proclaimed his innocence of the crime he never committed, even at the expense of having his appeals for parole denied for which an admission of guilt and contrition is virtually required.

Dorothy Day was a journalist, organizer, and the co-founder, with Peter Maurin, of the Catholic Worker Movement, the radical pacifist Catholic movement that sustained houses of hospitality, voluntary poverty, and a tradition of nonviolent civil disobedience that has continued for nearly a century. She was first arrested in 1917, at age 19, picketing the White House for women's suffrage with the Silent Sentinels — a sentence she served at the Occoquan Workhouse and described as her political baptism. She was arrested repeatedly across the next six decades.

In the 1950s she was jailed several times for refusing to take shelter during New York's Operation Alert civil-defense drills, an act of conscientious objection she defended as a refusal to lend the cooperation of the city to the rehearsal of nuclear war; her 1957 sentence was thirty days. In the summer of 1973, at age 75, she joined Cesar Chavez and the United Farm Workers on the picket lines in California's Central Valley in defiance of a court injunction against mass picketing of grape and lettuce growers. She was arrested with other UFW supporters and jailed for ten days at the Fresno County Jail. It was her last imprisonment.

She died in 1980. The Vatican opened her cause for canonization in 2000; she has been declared a Servant of God. Her arrests, taken together, span every major American radical movement of the 20th century — suffrage, IWW solidarity, antiwar, civil defense resistance, and the farm workers — making her one of the most consistently jailed political prisoners in U.S. history.

Frances Crowe was an American Quaker, longtime Western Massachusetts peace and anti-nuclear-power organizer, and one of the most prolific draft counselors of the Vietnam era — she counseled an estimated 2,000 conscientious objectors and draft resisters out of her Northampton home in the 1960s and early 1970s. She was a central organizer of the regional movement against the Vermont Yankee and Indian Point nuclear power plants, and of the Western Massachusetts opposition to U.S. military intervention from Vietnam through the Iraq wars.

She was arrested more than fifteen times for civil disobedience over the course of her life, almost all for short terms, with longer stretches at the Hampshire County Jail in Northampton. She was first arrested in 1972 (at age 53) for blocking Selective Service offices in protest of the Vietnam War; her last documented arrest came in November 2018 at age 99, when she sat in protest outside a TD Bank in Northampton against the bank's financing of the Dakota Access Pipeline. She wrote about her arrests, draft counseling, and Quaker pacifism in her 2014 memoir Finding My Radical Soul. She died on August 27, 2019 at age 100.

Civil-rights organizer (United Church of Christ Commission for Racial Justice) and leader of the Wilmington Ten, convicted on trumped-up charges of firebombing a white-owned store during 1971 racial unrest in Wilmington, NC. Originally sentenced to 25–29 years. The Black Panther Vol. 18 no.2 (1978); Amnesty International classed the group as political prisoners. The convictions were overturned in 1980 and the group pardoned as innocent in 2012. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v18 no.2; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Benjamin Chavis Jr. was a young minister and a representative of the United Church of Christ’s Commission for Racial Justice who went to Wilmington in early 1971 to support Black students organizing a school boycott amid escalating conflict over desegregation and unequal treatment in the public schools. He became associated with the local protest movement that drew national attention and was later referred to as the Wilmington Ten.

After unrest that included the February 1971 firebombing of Mike's Grocery and accusations of attacks on emergency responders, Chavis and nine others were prosecuted in 1972; a jury convicted them on October 17, 1972, and Chavis received a 34‑year sentence. James B. Hunt Jr. later commuted the group’s sentences, and Chavis was the last to be paroled (December 1979); in December 1980, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit overturned the convictions. Decades later, Beverly Perdue issued pardons of innocence (Dec. 31, 2012), formally clearing the Wilmington Ten.

Born in Oxford, NC. By 1971, at age 23, was UCC Commission for Racial Justice field organizer dispatched to Wilmington to support Black students boycotting segregated schools. Oldest of the Wilmington Ten and de facto leader. Received the longest sentence: 34 years. Imprisoned ~4.5 years, paroled December 1979. Convictions overturned 1980. Later: Executive Director NAACP (1993-94); National Director Million Man March (1995). Pardoned innocent 2012; received state compensation. Continues as journalist (Chavis Chronicles).

One of the Wilmington 10, convicted in 1972 on conspiracy and arson charges arising from the February 1971 firebombing of Mike's Grocery in Wilmington, North Carolina. Convictions of all ten were vacated by the Fourth Circuit in 1980 after recantations by prosecution witnesses, and Governor Bev Perdue granted pardons of innocence on December 31, 2012.

James “Bun” McKoy was one of the Black student activists swept into Wilmington’s 1971 school boycott and protests for educational equality during the city’s desegregation turmoil. He became one of the Wilmington Ten, a group whose legal case became emblematic of the era’s racial and political tensions.

McKoy was prosecuted in 1972 in connection with the firebombing of Mike’s Grocery and allegations that the group conspired to assault emergency responders. The Wilmington Ten were convicted on October 17, 1972, and McKoy received a 29‑year sentence. The convictions were overturned by the Fourth Circuit in 1980, and the group was later granted pardons of innocence in 2012. Wilmington native; convicted at age 19 with 29-year sentence (third-longest). Lived quietly in Wilmington post-release. Died November 10, 2023, age 69.

Wilmington native, age 19 at conviction. 29-year sentence. Died c. 1990, pardoned posthumously 2012. William “Joe” Wright Jr. was one of the Black student participants in Wilmington’s 1971 school boycott and activism during the city’s tense desegregation period. Wright became one of the Wilmington Ten, a group whose prosecution became one of the best-known civil-rights-era legal controversies in North Carolina.

Wright was charged with the group in relation to the February 1971 firebombing of Mike’s Grocery and a conspiracy allegation involving assaults on emergency responders. A jury convicted the Wilmington Ten on October 17, 1972; Wright received a 29‑year sentence. The convictions were overturned by the Fourth Circuit in 1980, and decades later the state issued pardons of innocence to the Wilmington Ten in 2012.

One of the Wilmington Ten, convicted on trumped-up firebombing/conspiracy charges from the 1971 Wilmington, NC unrest. The Black Panther Vol. 18 no.2 (1978). Convictions overturned 1980; group pardoned 2012. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v18 no.2; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Originally from Auburn, NY. White social worker, age 35 at time of arrest — the only woman and only white member of the Wilmington Ten. Convicted as accessory before the fact and conspiracy to assault emergency personnel; sentenced to 15 years. Paroled 1977. Died 2011, pardoned posthumously 2012.

Anne Sheppard (also reported in some records as “Ann Shepard”) was the only white and only female defendant among the Wilmington Ten. Sheppard was involved in the broader community context around the 1971 boycott and protests centered on educational equality and the treatment of Black students during Wilmington’s desegregation turmoil.

Sheppard was charged as an accessory before the fact in the burning of the building that housed Mike’s Grocery, while the nine male defendants faced charges including conspiracy to assault emergency personnel and burning the building. The Wilmington Ten were convicted on October 17, 1972; Sheppard received a 15‑year sentence. The convictions were later overturned in 1980, and the group ultimately received pardons of innocence in 2012.

RNA citizen from Milwaukee, age 29 at the time of the August 18, 1971 raid. Convicted of firing the shot that killed Lt. William L. Skinner. Sentenced to life imprisonment by the state of Mississippi. Husband of Tamu Sana (also arrested in the raid).

Born Richard Bullock Henry in Philadelphia. With his brother Milton (Gaidi Obadele) co-founded the Republic of New Afrika in Detroit in 1968 and became its first elected president of the Provisional Government. Murder charges from the 1971 Jackson raid were dropped (he was not at the scene). In 1973 federal court convicted him of conspiracy to assault a federal officer; sentenced to 12 years, served ~5-7. Paroled 1980. Earned PhD in political science from Temple University 1985; taught at Prairie View A&M and other HBCUs. Filed 1977 FOIA suit that exposed FBI COINTELPRO targeting of RNA. Founded N'COBRA (1987). Died 2010 of stroke in Atlanta, age 79. Imari Obadele was a co-founder of the Malcolm X Society, an advocate for reparations, and the president of Republic of New Afrika (RNA), a Black separatist group advocating for the liberation of Black people in America. In 1971, police and FBI agents raided an RNA house in Jackson, MS, with warrants to arrest four men. One policeman was killed and an FBI agent was wounded in an ensuing shoot-out. Obadele was not in the house but police arrested him nearby and charged him with murder. After seventeen months in prison, he was released, and the charge was dropped. However, federal authorities unfairly targeted Obadele and arrested him again, charging him with conspiracy to assault a Federal officer. Witnesses at the trial testified that they heard Obadele, on an earlier occasion, tell the policeman who was slain in the shoot-out that he would "be ready" for the police if they came to the RNA house. Obadele was convicted and sentenced to twelve years in prison, ultimately serving five. He filed a civil suit against the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
which resulted in the release of government documents confirming that the RNA had been targeted for subversion by the covert and often illegal Counter Intelligence Program of the FBI. After prison, Obadele went on to earn a PhD in political science from Temple University. He became a professor at Prairie View A&M University. Later, in 1987, Obadele and Chokwe Lumumba formed the National Coalition of Blacks for Reparations in America (N'COBRA), an organization dedicated to seeking financial compensation for the descendants of former slaves in the United States.
RNA citizen from Milwaukee, age 24 at the time of the raid. Married to Hekima Ana. Held about 10 months in Mississippi custody before release.

Father Michael Doyle was an Irish-born Catholic priest of the Diocese of Camden, New Jersey, longtime pastor at Sacred Heart Church in South Camden, and one of the Camden 28 defendants. He was one of more than twenty defendants arrested in the early hours of August 22, 1971 during the FBI surveillance and capture of the Camden draft-board raid in progress. He spent brief pretrial detention after the arrest, and the case proceeded to trial in spring 1973 in U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey. On May 20, 1973 a Camden federal jury acquitted all 28 defendants on all counts — the first complete legal victory for the anti-war movement after dozens of Catholic Left draft-board actions. He went on to a 50-year ministry in South Camden focused on housing, food access, and immigrant rights. He died on November 23, 2022, age 88.

Apache/Chicano indigenous rights activist convicted in California of the murder of two police officers, a case supporters say was a frame-up tied to his organizing. Held at Kern Valley State Prison.

Luis V. Rodriguez was an Apache/Chicano activist. He was raised in an atmosphere of political and social involvement and later joined the Brown Berets, a Chicano-Native American militant organization, which formed against racism and other social injustices. Framed and convicted of killing two California Highway Patrol officers, Luis fought with determination to prove his innocence for 37 years.

He faced constant violence from guards at Pelican Bay State Prison where he was originally incarcerated; when he was beaten to the point of not be able to walk anymore, he was not provided a wheelchair or cane as a further act of crulty. He later was moved to other prisons, fearing retaliation for a pending lawsuit and FBI investigation, and eventually died in 2016 at age 60.

Chicano political prisoner held in California's Pelican Bay State Prison, identified in PFOC Breakthrough magazine as part of the network of Chicano/Mexicano political prisoners supported by anti-imperialist organizing. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

Jesuit priest, age 35 at indictment, based at Woodstock Religious College, NYC; native of Jersey City who entered the Society of Jesus in 1956. Had already taken public responsibility (with the East Coast Conspiracy to Save Lives) for the February 1970 Philadelphia draft-board and Washington GE-office raids. At trial he declared 'I ripped up those files with my hands.' Acquitted in 1973.

Youngest documented member of the Camden 28, age 20 at the 1971 indictment. Graduate of Immaculate Heart Academy, Bergen County NJ; her antiwar involvement began with the 1968 McCarthy campaign. Worked as a children's librarian. Acquitted with all defendants in the 1973 jury-nullification trial.

Boston native, age 33 at indictment; ordained a Franciscan priest in 1965. Founded Liberty Village, a drug-treatment center in Jersey City (1967), and was later married with two children. Former director of training for NJ's Drug Education Program, suspended without pay at his arrest. Acquitted in 1973.

Massachusetts native, age 23 at indictment; a draft and military counselor who left his conscientious-objector alternate service in January 1971 and moved to Dorchester for community and movement work. Acquitted in 1973.

Jesuit priest and NYC native, age 34 at indictment; entered the Society of Jesus in 1955, ordained 1968, taught Classics and Theology. A member of the New York 8, he ran a GI coffeehouse near Fort Devens, MA, worked as a draft counselor, and was a national coordinator of the Harrisburg Defense Committee. Acquitted in 1973.

From Ho-Ho-Kus, NJ, age 20 at indictment; a 1969 Immaculate Heart Academy graduate and National Honor Society president, NJ district coordinator for the 1968 McCarthy campaign. Attended Wellesley College, was active in Boston's Paulist Center, and did community work in Dorchester. Acquitted in 1973.

Lutheran minister, age 39 at indictment, ordained 1958. The only Protestant clergyman among the Camden 28. Worked with Appalachians near Cincinnati, helped develop Columbus (Ohio) ECCO anti-poverty foundation, and was Outreach Director of Camden's EPOC. Acquitted in 1973.

Bryn Mawr-educated daughter of an Illinois banker and Republican state legislator who taught with the Peace Corps in Guatemala, then organized with Jobs or Income Now in Cleveland and Ann Arbor SDS, where she became Bill Ayers's partner. Joined Weatherman after the June 1969 SDS split. Killed at age 28 on March 6, 1970 in the Greenwich Village townhouse explosion at 18 West 11th Street while assembling, with Terry Robbins, a nail bomb intended for an enlisted-soldiers' dance at Fort Dix; her body was identified only by a fingertip.

James K. Holley, 20, was one of the Carbondale 3 — Southern Illinois University students and Black Panthers arrested after the November 12, 1970 pre-dawn police siege of the Panther house at 401 North Washington Street in Carbondale, Illinois, in which university, state and local police fired 778 bullets into the building during a nearly three-hour standoff. All six occupants were charged with attempted murder and aggravated battery of a police officer; Holley, Michael Johnson and Leonard Thomas were arrested and prosecuted as the Carbondale 3. In the summer of 1971 a Jackson County jury acquitted them on all 41 counts, with the People's Law Office (Jeff Haas, Michael Deutsch, Flint Taylor, Steve White) defending, and charges against the other three were dropped. The siege is the subject of the documentary 778 Bullets. How long the three were held before trial has not been located.

Leonard Thomas, 20, was one of the Carbondale 3 — Southern Illinois University students and Black Panthers arrested after the November 12, 1970 pre-dawn police siege of the Panther house at 401 North Washington Street in Carbondale, Illinois, in which police fired 778 bullets into the building. Charged with attempted murder and aggravated battery of a police officer alongside James K. Holley and Michael Johnson, he was acquitted on all 41 counts by a Jackson County jury in the summer of 1971, with the People's Law Office defending. The siege is the subject of the documentary 778 Bullets. How long the three were held before trial has not been located.

David Sylvan Fine was an 18-year-old University of Wisconsin-Madison student in 1970 and one of the four-man New Years Gang who carried out the August 24, 1970 ammonium-nitrate truck bombing of Sterling Hall on the UW-Madison campus, killing researcher Robert Fassnacht. He fled to Canada with co-defendant Leo Burt and lived underground for over five years. He was arrested on January 7, 1976 in San Rafael, California. He pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in Wisconsin and was sentenced to 7 years in federal prison. He served 3 years and was released in 1979. (Leo Burt remains a fugitive as of 2025 — the longest-held FBI Most Wanted listing in U.S. history.)

Karleton Lewis Karl Armstrong was a 23-year-old University of Wisconsin-Madison student in 1970 and the principal organizer of the August 24, 1970 ammonium-nitrate truck bombing of Sterling Hall on the UW-Madison campus. The four-man New Years Gang — Karl, his younger brother Dwight Armstrong, David Fine, and Leo Burt — had identified the Army Mathematics Research Center on the second through fourth floors of Sterling Hall as the principal U.S. academic provider of strategic-bombing target analysis for the Vietnam War. The 2,000-pound ANFO truck bomb detonated at 3:42 a.m.; the building was largely empty but a graduate-student researcher, Robert Fassnacht, was working in a basement laboratory and was killed. Three other people were injured.

Karl fled to Canada and lived underground for nearly two years before being arrested in Toronto in February 1972. He was extradited to the United States, pleaded guilty in September 1973 to second-degree murder and other charges, and was sentenced to 23 years in Wisconsin state prison. He served 7 years and was paroled in 1980. He has spent his life since in Madison.

Twymon Ford Myers was a Black Liberation Army member from New York sought in connection with police shootings, armed robberies and other BLA actions. Added to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list (No. 319) on September 28, 1973, he was killed on November 14, 1973 at age 23 in a shootout with FBI agents and New York police in the Bronx — he was never arrested, tried or convicted.

James Reynolds Mendoza was a 19-year-old Chicano from Milwaukee's Southside held in the city jail for the July 1974 shooting deaths of off-duty policemen Robert Riley and Thomas Matulis, who were killed — possibly with their own guns — after a drunken altercation involving Matulis's own brother and his drinking companions. Mendoza was arrested at his cousin's house fourteen hours later. A witness who saw the shooting from ten feet said she knew the assailant by name and that it was not Mendoza and that no Mexican-Americans were at the scene; twenty other witnesses also failed to link him to the shooting, while police ransacked homes and searched without warrants for evidence against him. The Black Panther reported his case as that of a brother unjustly held while the poor white and Chicano Southside was thrown into upheaval. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974); the later disposition of his case has not been located.

Chester Jackson, 30, was one of the four Angola prisoners charged in the April 1972 killing of guard Brent Miller alongside Herman Wallace, Albert Woodfox and Gilbert Montegut. At the start of the January 1974 Baton Rouge trial he had what The Black Panther called a sudden change of heart and became the prosecution's star witness; his own trial was severed and was expected to proceed on a lesser charge. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, 1974 run; his later disposition has not been located.

Gilbert Montegut, 23, was one of the four Angola prisoners charged in the April 1972 killing of prison guard Brent Miller — the case that produced the Angola 3. Tried alongside Herman Wallace in Baton Rouge beginning January 7, 1974, in a trial The Black Panther described as marked with contradictions, inconsistencies and surprise — the fourth defendant, Chester Jackson, turned prosecution witness at its start — Montegut was acquitted while Wallace was convicted. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, 1974 run.

Joyce Guerrero was a 27-year-old Potawatomi woman and mother of two who, The Black Panther reported (September 14, 1974), was the only person sentenced over the confiscation of Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) documents during the November 1972 "Trail of Broken Treaties" occupation of BIA headquarters in Washington, D.C. Her role in the demonstration had been caring for the 75 to 100 children left without shelter when promised accommodations fell through. After she returned home to Topeka, Kansas, FBI agents charged her with receiving, concealing and retaining stolen BIA documents — though, supporters noted, no BIA property was found on her person or in her possession — and an all-White jury convicted her on May 22, 1973. She was sentenced to nine months in jail and three years' probation, and later given additional jail time for "willfully" failing to appear at an earlier pretrial hearing.

Bruce "Deacon" Washington was a 26-year-old member of the Black Panther Party in Oakland who was shot in the back and killed on October 26, 1974 while shielding children during a shooting at a teen dance held at the Party's Community Learning Center (Son of Man Temple, 6118 East 14th Street). Three people, including a 12-year-old, were also wounded; Washington died after more than eight hours of emergency surgery at Highland Hospital. As The Black Panther reported (November 2, 1974), Party spokesperson Elaine Brown said the Party believed the attack had been provoked by police to disrupt the Center's community work.

The Black Panther of August 10, 1974 reported that a Bruce Washington — presumably the same Oakland Party member — was the fourth B.P.P. member charged, on two misdemeanor counts, in the wake of the Fox nightclub arrests of Huey P. Newton and seven other Panthers that month.

Charles Wyche was a member of the Baltimore Black Panther Party tried in April 1971 in the prosecution over the torture-killing of Eugene Leroy Anderson. Eugene Leroy Anderson, a 20-year-old Panther sympathizer, was tortured and shot to death in July 1969 and his body left in Baltimore's Leakin Park, where it was found on October 27, 1969. Maryland authorities charged some 21 members of the Baltimore Black Panther Party — a prosecution widely seen as an attempt to destroy the chapter — but no one was ultimately convicted of the killing except one defendant, who was released after four years by Governor Marvin Mandel.

Irving Young was a member of the Baltimore Black Panther Party whom police alleged had driven Eugene Leroy Anderson and his killers to Leakin Park in July 1969; his case went to trial in November 1970. Eugene Leroy Anderson, a 20-year-old Panther sympathizer, was tortured and shot to death in July 1969 and his body left in Baltimore's Leakin Park, where it was found on October 27, 1969. Maryland authorities charged some 21 members of the Baltimore Black Panther Party — a prosecution widely seen as an attempt to destroy the chapter — but no one was ultimately convicted of the killing except one defendant, who was released after four years by Governor Marvin Mandel.

Omaha activist and member of the National Committee to Combat Fascism (a BPP affiliate), convicted with David Rice of the 1970 bombing death of a policeman on the testimony of a 15-year-old who admitted planting the bomb; The Black Panther Vol. 14 no.23 (1976). One of the 'Omaha Two,' he (Ed Poindexter) remained imprisoned for decades. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v14 no.23; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Fleeta Drumgo was a Black prisoner at Soledad Prison in California and one of the three men known as the Soledad Brothers — alongside George Jackson and John Cluchette — who in February 1970 were charged with the murder of Soledad guard John Mills. Mills had been beaten to death and thrown from a tier days after a white guard in the Soledad yard shot and killed three Black prisoners during a fight. There was no physical evidence connecting any of the three men to the killing. The case became an international cause and the focus of the Soledad Brothers Defense Committee, with Angela Davis as one of its central organizers. After George Jackson was killed by guards at San Quentin on August 21, 1971, three days before the trial was set to begin, Drumgo and Cluchette were tried together. On March 27, 1972, the jury acquitted both men of all charges. Drumgo was released and continued political organizing in Oakland. He was killed in an unrelated 1979 shooting at age 33.

Arthur Turco Jr. was a New York movement lawyer indicted on May 1, 1970 for taking part in the torture and murder of Eugene Leroy Anderson, in the Baltimore Black Panther case. Eugene Leroy Anderson, a 20-year-old Panther sympathizer, was tortured and shot to death in July 1969 and his body left in Baltimore's Leakin Park, where it was found on October 27, 1969. Maryland authorities charged some 21 members of the Baltimore Black Panther Party — a prosecution widely seen as an attempt to destroy the chapter — but no one was ultimately convicted of the killing except one defendant, who was released after four years by Governor Marvin Mandel. Turco spent about a year in the Baltimore City Jail awaiting trial; his trial ran June 16 to July 3, 1971 before Judge James W. Murphy and ended in a mistrial (the jury reportedly stood 10-2 for conviction). He then accepted an offer to plead guilty to a misdemeanor and was freed on time served; William Kunstler took part in his defense.

Charles Wakefield was a 21-year-old Black man in Greenville, South Carolina, convicted in 1976 of murdering Greenville County Sheriff's Lt. Frank Looper and Looper's father, Rufus, during an alleged armed robbery on January 31, 1975 — and given a mandatory death sentence on a record of conflicting testimony. Indicted nine months after the killings, he was convicted on the word of two county-jail inmates who were offered reduced sentences and of an alleged accomplice, Wyatt Earp Harper, himself indicted as an accessory; three prosecution witnesses gave conflicting descriptions and a published composite drawing did not resemble him. A survey of Greenville County found that 72 percent of Black residents believed he had been framed. Documented in The Black Panther (July 24, 1976).

22-year-old Black community activist in Santa Ana convicted in a 1972 police frame-up of shooting two market clerks after he had organized against alcohol sales to minors; The Black Panther Vol. 14 no.2 (1975) reports his own attorney betrayed and testified against him, his first trial hung, and he drew a 30-year sentence and appealed. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v14 no.2; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Jamal Joseph, born Eddie Joseph in The Bronx in 1953, was at age 16 the youngest defendant in the 1969 Panther 21 case (acquitted with the rest of the Panther 21 in May 1971). He was convicted in U.S. District Court in 1983 as an accessory after the fact in connection with the October 20, 1981 Brink s expropriation in Nyack, New York and the alleged 1979 liberation of Assata Shakur. He served eight years at the federal penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas, where he completed two college degrees and began the writing career that has made him a major American figure since release. He has been a tenured professor of film at the Columbia University School of the Arts since 2005 and chaired the schools Graduate Film MFA program.

Sundiata Acoli, born Clark Squire in Decatur, Texas in 1937, is a former NASA mathematician, member of the Harlem chapter of the Black Panther Party, and Black Liberation Army soldier. He was one of the original Panther 21 defendants — twenty-one New York Panthers acquitted in May 1971 of conspiring to bomb New York police stations. After the Panther 21 acquittal he went underground with the BLA. On May 2, 1973 he was a passenger in the car driven by Assata Shakur on the New Jersey Turnpike when state troopers pulled them over; in the ensuing shootout New Jersey State Trooper Werner Foerster was killed and BLA member Zayd Malik Shakur was killed. He was convicted of Trooper Foersters murder in 1974 and sentenced to life plus 30 years in New Jersey state prison.

He was repeatedly denied parole over the next four decades despite multiple clean disciplinary records and intervention by national civil-rights organizations. The Jericho Movement, of which he was a co-founder in 1998, made him one of its central campaigns. On May 11, 2022 the New Jersey Supreme Court ordered him paroled, ruling that the parole board had abused its discretion in continuing to deny release. He was released on May 26, 2022, age 85, after 49 years of imprisonment.

Joan Bird was a 19-year-old nursing student and Black Panther Party member when she was arrested on January 17, 1969 in connection with a Harlem incident in which NYPD officers exchanged gunfire with three men in a car; she was beaten in custody and the photograph of her bruised face became one of the most widely circulated images of the case. She was charged in the April 2, 1969 Panther 21 indictment as one of two women among the defendants (the other was Afeni Shakur) and was held at the Womens House of Detention in Greenwich Village on $100,000 bail. She was one of the 13 defendants who went to trial and was acquitted with the others on May 13, 1971.

Susan Marie Parker was a 21-year-old member of Students for a Democratic Society from Colorado Springs who was jailed for civil contempt by the federal grand jury in Denver investigating the dynamiting of Public Service Company transmission towers — the sabotage investigation (18 U.S.C. § 2153) at the center of the Cameron Bishop case; press accounts described her as an alleged friend of Bishop, then a fugitive believed to be in Canada. Called before the grand jury on April 1, 1969, she refused to answer on Fifth Amendment grounds, arguing among other things that answers could expose her to prosecution for an extraditable offense in Canada. Judge Alfred Arraj entered an immunity order on April 2; when she still refused, she was found in civil contempt on April 3, 1969 and committed to custody until she testified. Contemporaneous AP coverage preserved in Colorado State University's Collection on Student Unrest records her wavering under confinement — at one point announcing through counsel that she would testify "due to the coercion of incarceration" and a "decline in mental health," then changing her mind again. The Tenth Circuit affirmed the contempt in June 1969 (In the Matter of the Grand Jury and Susan Marie Parker, 411 F.2d 1067), while holding she had to be released once the grand jury expired. How long she ultimately remained jailed has not been located.

Mark Clark was a 22-year-old leader of the Peoria, Illinois chapter of the Black Panther Party. Born in Peoria in 1947, he had organized the chapters Free Breakfast for Children program. On the night of December 3-4, 1969, he traveled to Chicago with other Panthers to attend a meeting at Fred Hamptons West Side apartment.

In the predawn hours of December 4, 1969, fourteen members of the Cook County States Attorneys office, working from a floor plan supplied by FBI informant William ONeal, conducted a no-knock raid on the apartment. Clark was killed by a single gunshot to the chest as he sat in a chair near the door, in what the official autopsy and ballistics reconstruction later established was the first shot fired in the raid — by police, not by Panthers, despite official initial claims of a Panther shootout. Fred Hampton was killed in his bed minutes later. A federal civil-rights lawsuit by the survivors and the Hampton and Clark families was eventually settled in 1982 for $1.85 million, paid jointly by the federal government, Cook County, and the City of Chicago. The Jericho Movement lists Clark among its ancestor political prisoners.

Ronald Bridgeforth was a Black Panther Party member in San Francisco who spent more than forty years underground. In September 1968 he was arrested after a confrontation with police at a White Front discount store in San Francisco and pleaded guilty to assault with a deadly weapon; in 1969, rather than face sentencing, he fled and disappeared. Living under the name Cole Jordan, he earned bachelor's and master's degrees, raised a family, and worked for years as a community-college counselor in Michigan. In January 2007 he was charged in absentia as the ninth defendant in the San Francisco 8 case — the revived prosecution of former Panthers over the August 29, 1971 shotgun killing of SFPD Sergeant John Young at Ingleside station — while the eight others were arrested across the country. After the SF8 case largely collapsed, Bridgeforth surrendered voluntarily in San Francisco in November 2011, telling the press he had come back to account for his past and live openly. The murder charge was not pursued; he pleaded guilty to the 1968 assault charge and in March 2012, at age 67, was sentenced to a year in county jail. Reconstructed from coverage of the 2007 San Francisco 8 arrests and his 2011 surrender.

Bob Graf was a 25-year-old editor of The Catholic Radical and one of the Milwaukee 14. After serving 14 months in Wisconsin state prison he became a longtime Milwaukee Catholic Worker peace organizer and writer.
Doug Marvy was a 27-year-old draft-resistance organizer and one of the Milwaukee 14. He served 14 months in Wisconsin state prison after the September 24, 1968 draft-board raid.
Fred Ojile was a 23-year-old Minneapolis draft counselor and one of the Milwaukee 14. He served 14 months in Wisconsin state prison after the September 24, 1968 draft-board raid.

Jerry Gardner was a 24-year-old Marquette University graduate student and one of the Milwaukee 14. He served 14 months in Wisconsin state prison after the September 24, 1968 draft-board raid and continued anti-war organizing in Wisconsin.
Jon Higgenbotham was a 27-year-old minister and one of the Milwaukee 14. He served 14 months in Wisconsin state prison after the September 24, 1968 draft-board raid.

Michael Cullen was a 26-year-old Irish-born director of Casa Maria House of Hospitality, the Milwaukee Catholic Worker, and one of the principal organizers of the Milwaukee 14 raid on September 24, 1968. After serving 14 months in Wisconsin state prison he was deported to Ireland in 1974 in connection with his immigration status. He continued Catholic Worker peace organizing in Ireland for the rest of his life.

Don Cotton was a 24-year-old co-chairman of Students for a Democratic Society at Saint Louis University and one of the Milwaukee 14 — the Catholic Left affinity group that on September 24, 1968 entered the Brumder Building in downtown Milwaukee, removed approximately 10,000 1-A draft files from the nine Wisconsin Selective Service boards housed there, carried them to a public square, and burned them with homemade napalm in front of waiting reporters. The Milwaukee 14 were tried in Wisconsin state court for burglary, arson, and theft and convicted; on June 6, 1969 each was sentenced to 2 years state prison (with parole eligibility at 14 months).

Charles Bursey was a member of the Black Panther Party in Oakland, later well known for serving meals in the Party's Free Breakfast for Children Program. He was one of the Panthers present during the April 6, 1968 confrontation with Oakland police — two days after Dr. King's assassination — in which police killed 17-year-old Bobby Hutton and wounded Eldridge Cleaver and Warren Wells. Indicted on two counts of attempted murder and two counts of assault with a deadly weapon, he was held in the Alameda County Jail and then convicted on all four counts on August 7, 1969. The Black Panther newspaper called him "a black political prisoner in the Alameda County Jail."

Donnell Lankford was a member of the Black Panther Party arrested in the April 6, 1968 gun battle between Panthers and Oakland police in which 17-year-old Bobby Hutton was killed. Indicted on two counts of attempted murder and two counts of assault with a deadly weapon, he was tried jointly with Terry Cotton (People v. Lankford and Cotton, Alameda County Superior Court No. 42287); both were convicted of the assault charges and acquitted of attempted murder. His case was later cited in In re Wells as part of the prosecution's pattern of striking Black jurors — no Black person served on any of the three related Panther juries.

Eldridge Cleaver was the Black Panther Party's Minister of Information and the author of Soul on Ice (1968), one of the foundational texts of Black liberation literature. He had spent most of the previous decade in Folsom and San Quentin on convictions for assault and rape (convictions he later disavowed and which independent historians have substantially questioned); he joined the Panthers shortly after his 1966 parole. On April 6, 1968, two days after the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., he and 17-year-old Panther Bobby Hutton were involved in a shootout with Oakland police; Hutton was killed by police while attempting to surrender, and Cleaver was wounded and arrested. Facing reimprisonment as a parole violator, he jumped bail in November 1968 and fled first to Cuba, then to Algeria, then to France. He returned voluntarily to the United States in 1975 and surrendered; the original charges were eventually reduced and he served no further significant time.

John L. Scott was a member of the Black Panther Party and the eighth person indicted over the April 6, 1968 West Oakland gun battle in which 17-year-old Bobby Hutton was killed. Co-defendant Terry Cotton recalled that "Donnell [Lankford], John L. Scott and I were the first to be arrested." He was charged with the group on two counts of attempted murder and two counts of assault with a deadly weapon. The most thinly documented of the eight — absent even from the Party's own February 1970 prisoner roster — he has no individually recorded trial disposition.

Warren William Wells was a captain and sergeant-at-arms of the Black Panther Party who was wounded in the April 6, 1968 West Oakland gun battle in which the police killed 17-year-old Bobby Hutton and wounded Eldridge Cleaver. Indicted with seven co-defendants on attempted-murder and assault charges, Wells was tried separately; after two trials ended in hung juries, a third found him guilty of assault with a deadly weapon while acquitting him of attempted murder, and he was given an indeterminate term of 1 to 15 years. The conviction was later reversed on appeal over the composition of the Alameda County grand jury (In re Wells, 1971). He became a leader of the California prison movement and a co-author of the 1970 Folsom Manifesto, and died in 2001. (Not to be confused with the NFL player of the same name.)

Wendell Wade (also spelled Wendel Wade in Party publications) was a captain in the Black Panther Party, arrested in connection with the April 6, 1968 confrontation with Oakland police in which 17-year-old Bobby Hutton was killed and Eldridge Cleaver and Warren Wells were wounded. He was among the group indicted by the Alameda County grand jury on two counts of attempted murder and two counts of assault with a deadly weapon, and was listed by name among the April 6, 1968 defendants in the Black Panther newspaper's February 1970 roster of political prisoners. (A car co-registered to Wade figured in the search-and-seizure question later decided in Cleaver v. Superior Court.) The disposition of his individual case is not documented in available sources.

Danny Seals, then 21 and from Auburn, California, was a U.S. Army soldier and one of the "Presidio 27" — the stockade prisoners at the Presidio of San Francisco who, on October 14, 1968, staged a sit-down protest against brutal conditions and the killing of a fellow prisoner, Richard Bunch, who had been shot in the back by a guard three days earlier. Singing "We Shall Overcome" and reading out a list of grievances, the men were charged with mutiny, a capital offense. On appeal in June 1970 the mutiny convictions were reduced to willful disobedience, and the defendants were released after about eighteen months.
