Co-defendant of Fred Ahmed Evans in the Glenville Shootout — the July 23, 1968 armed confrontation in the Glenville neighborhood of Cleveland, Ohio between the Black Nationalists of New Libya (a militant Black-nationalist group led by Evans) and Cleveland police. Three police officers, three Black militants, and one Black civilian were killed in the gunfight, which sparked five days of uprising in the city. Federal and state authorities prosecuted the surviving militants in what became one of the harshest Black-nationalist prosecutions of the era. Hardrick was 17 at the time of the shootout. Adjudicated delinquent in juvenile court and held at Mansfield Youth Center until age 21.

Co-defendant of Fred Ahmed Evans in the Glenville Shootout — the July 23, 1968 armed confrontation in the Glenville neighborhood of Cleveland, Ohio between the Black Nationalists of New Libya (a militant Black-nationalist group led by Evans) and Cleveland police. Three police officers, three Black militants, and one Black civilian were killed in the gunfight, which sparked five days of uprising in the city. Federal and state authorities prosecuted the surviving militants in what became one of the harshest Black-nationalist prosecutions of the era. Donald, age 19 at the time of the shootout, was convicted in August 1969 of three counts of first-degree murder and four counts of second-degree murder. Sentenced to seven consecutive life terms with a minimum of 110 years.

Co-defendant of Fred Ahmed Evans in the Glenville Shootout — the July 23, 1968 armed confrontation in the Glenville neighborhood of Cleveland, Ohio between the Black Nationalists of New Libya (a militant Black-nationalist group led by Evans) and Cleveland police. Karl H. Meyer is a pacifist and long-running direct-action organizer associated with the Catholic Worker Movement and with war-tax resistance campaigns. His activism has emphasized nonviolent protest, voluntary poverty and mutual aid, and highly visible “public witness” actions meant to force attention to war, capital punishment, and government policy. He has also been involved in experimental protest tactics tied to tax resistance and public demonstrations.

Meyer’s arrests are a consistent feature of his activism rather than an exception. He participated in the 1961 peace march to Moscow and later staged long-distance protests (including a death-penalty protest walk dragging a mock electric chair). He has described decades of repeated arrests during protests and civil-disobedience actions, alongside sustained conflict with the Internal Revenue Service over tax-resistance tactics. In recent years he has remained active in Nashville, including an arrest in 2024 after intentionally sleeping on the Tennessee state-capitol grounds as a protest against a law escalating penalties for public camping. Son of former U.S. Representative William H. Meyer of Vermont, born in a cabin in northern Wisconsin. At age 19 he attempted to open a Catholic Worker house of hospitality in Washington, D.C.; on July 12, 1957 he met Dorothy Day and Ammon Hennacy at the Chrystie Street Catholic Worker. After witnessing the imprisonment of war tax resister Eroseanna Robinson, he vowed never to pay federal income tax again, pioneering the W-4 extra-allowances method to block withholding. He served two years in federal prison for tax resistance and shorter terms in 20 different jails. In 1984 he defied the IRS "frivolous filing" penalty by filing a frivolous return every day that year, was assessed $140,000 in penalties, and coined the term "cabbage patch resistance."

Herman Ferguson was a New York City public-school principal, a co-founder of the Organization of Afro-American Unity with Malcolm X in 1964, and a longtime leader of the Republic of New Afrika movement. After Malcolm Xs assassination in February 1965, Ferguson became one of the most prominent organizers of the radical Black liberation network that grew out of the OAAU and the Revolutionary Action Movement.

In June 1967 he was arrested by the New York Police Departments Bureau of Special Services and charged with conspiracy to murder Roy Wilkins of the NAACP and Whitney Young of the National Urban League. The principal evidence at trial came from a paid NYPD informant. Ferguson was convicted in 1968 and sentenced to three and a half to seven years in New York state prison. While free pending appeal he fled the United States with his wife Iyaluua Ferguson and settled in Cooperative Republic of Guyana, where they remained for twenty years. He returned voluntarily to New York in April 1989 and surrendered. He served roughly three years in New York state prison and was released in 1992.

He spent his last decades organizing for the freedom of U.S. political prisoners, serving as a co-chair of the Jericho Movement and on the board of the Malcolm X Commemoration Committee. He died on October 14, 2014, age 93.

Detroit man convicted of first-degree murder in 1966 at age 19 and sentenced to life; The Black Panther Vol. 15 no.26 (1976) reports prosecution witnesses had since admitted they were coerced into lying, yet Michigan refused a new trial. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v15 no.26; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Frank Big Black Smith was a 300-pound African-American prisoner at Attica Correctional Facility in upstate New York who became the principal internal security organizer of the September 9-13, 1971 Attica prison rebellion — still the bloodiest prison uprising in U.S. history. With 1,281 of Atticas approximately 2,200 prisoners, he took control of the prison and held 42 prison staff as hostages over four days, demanding political and human-rights reforms. After negotiations broke down, New York State Police retook the prison on Governor Nelson Rockefellers orders on September 13, 1971; 43 people died — 10 prison staff and 33 prisoners — almost all by state-police gunfire.

In the immediate aftermath he was singled out for retaliatory torture by guards: he was stripped naked, forced to lie on a table for hours with a football placed under his chin and was told that if he dropped the football he would be killed. He was burned with cigarettes and beaten. He was held in solitary confinement for six months. He was released on parole in 1973 after 8.5 years of a 10-15 year sentence for an unrelated New York City dice-game robbery. After his release he became a longtime substance-abuse counselor and the lead plaintiff in the 26-year class-action civil-rights lawsuit by Attica survivors that eventually settled for $12 million in 2000. He died in 2004, age 70.

David J. Miller was a 24-year-old Catholic Worker pacifist and the first person prosecuted under the August 1965 amendment to the Selective Service Act criminalizing destruction of a draft card. On October 15, 1965, at a rally outside the Armed Forces Induction Center on Whitehall Street in lower Manhattan, Miller burned his draft card with a borrowed lighter; FBI agents arrested him three days later. He was convicted in February 1966 and sentenced to 30 months in federal prison. The Second Circuit upheld his conviction (367 F.2d 72), and the Supreme Court declined to take the case, instead later upholding the law in United States v. O'Brien (1968). Miller remained free on bail until June 1968, when he began serving and ultimately did 22 months in federal prison.

Thomas Charles Cornell was an American pacifist organizer, ordained Catholic deacon, longtime member of the Catholic Worker Movement, and a co-founder of the Catholic Peace Fellowship. As a young Catholic Worker in the early 1960s, he played a central role in initiating the first organized U.S. opposition to the Vietnam War. On July 29, 1965, just weeks after Congress passed the new federal law making destruction of a draft card a crime punishable by five years in prison, Cornell publicly burned his draft card at a New York City rally — an act of civil disobedience explicitly designed to test the constitutionality of the new statute.

On November 6, 1965 he again publicly burned his draft card, this time alongside David Miller, A. J. Muste, Dorothy Day, and three others, at an even larger New York rally. He was prosecuted federally and was convicted in 1968. The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the draft-card-burning statute the same year (United States v. O'Brien, 1968). Cornell served six months in the Federal Correctional Institution at Danbury, Connecticut.

After his release he spent the remainder of his life as a Catholic Worker organizer, a co-editor of the Catholic Worker newspaper, and a columnist on labor and Christian-pacifist politics. He was ordained a permanent deacon of the Roman Catholic Church in 1988. He died on August 1, 2022 at age 88.

June Johnson was a 15-year-old Greenwood, Mississippi SNCC volunteer when she was arrested on June 9, 1963 at the Winona Trailways bus station with Fannie Lou Hamer, Annell Ponder, and others returning from a citizenship workshop. Beaten by officers in Montgomery County jail despite her age — they struck her with blackjacks until her hair fell out — Johnson became a lifelong civil-rights organizer. She continued with SNCC and the MFDP through the 1964 Freedom Summer and Atlantic City convention, and served as a school board member and longtime activist in Washington, D.C.

Stokely Carmichael (later Kwame Ture) was a Trinidadian-American civil rights organizer who became chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee in 1966 and popularized the slogan 'Black Power' that summer in Greenwood, Mississippi. He was arrested for the first time as a 19-year-old Freedom Rider in 1961 and served 49 days in Mississippi's Parchman Penitentiary in solitary confinement, in maximum security with the men on death row. He was arrested at least 32 more times over the following decade for civil rights organizing. He spent his last decades in Conakry, Guinea, organizing through the All-African People's Revolutionary Party.

Larry Michael Spain, known as Johnny Spain, was the only one of the San Quentin Six convicted of murder for the events of August 21, 1971. Born to a white mother and Black father in 1949 in Mississippi, raised in California after his mother sent him north to escape rural anti-Black violence, he was sentenced to life in 1967 at age 17 for murder during a robbery. Inside he became close to George Jackson and a member of the Black Guerrilla Family. He was convicted in 1976 of two counts of murder of guards Frank DeLeon and Jere Graham at San Quentin during the August 21, 1971 incident. The conviction was overturned by the Ninth Circuit in 1985 on the grounds that the trial judge had unconstitutionally ordered him chained to his courtroom seat. The state declined to retry. He was paroled in 1988 and lived in California until his death on March 6, 2008.

Black Panther Party member and one of the 'San Quentin 6,' tried for the events of Aug. 21, 1971 in San Quentin's Adjustment Center on the day George Jackson was killed; The Black Panther Vol. 15 (1976) covers the roughly 16-month trial, in which he was defended by attorney Charles Garry. Spain alone among the six was convicted of murder (a conviction later overturned in 1988). [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), Vol. 15 (1976); digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

George Lester Jackson was a Black revolutionary, author, and Field Marshal of the Black Panther Party — and the most influential Black political prisoner of his generation. Sentenced in 1961 at age 18 to one year to life for his alleged role in a $70 gas station robbery, he served the remaining ten years of his life behind bars, much of it in solitary confinement at Soledad and San Quentin. From inside, he co-founded the Black Guerrilla Family in 1966 and became a Field Marshal of the BPP in 1970. His prison letters, published in 1970 as Soledad Brother, became one of the foundational texts of the Black liberation movement, selling hundreds of thousands of copies and translated worldwide. His second book, Blood in My Eye, was completed days before his death and published posthumously in 1972.

In January 1970, after a white guard at Soledad shot and killed three Black prisoners during a yard fight, another guard, John Mills, was beaten to death and thrown from a tier. Jackson, along with Fleeta Drumgo and John Cluchette — known as the Soledad Brothers — were charged with the killing despite no physical evidence connecting them to it. The case became an international cause. On August 7, 1970, Jacksons 17-year-old brother Jonathan Jackson stormed the Marin County Courthouse in an attempt to free his brother, taking a judge and three jurors hostage; Jonathan, the judge, and two prisoners died in the resulting shootout.

On August 21, 1971, three days before he was scheduled to stand trial for the Mills killing, George Jackson was killed by guards at San Quentin in an alleged escape attempt that has been widely disputed in the decades since. He was 29 years old. The killing triggered the Attica prison rebellion three weeks later. Drumgo and Cluchette were acquitted at trial in 1972.

In February 1966, 19-year-old Barry Bondhus of Big Lake, Minnesota, dumped two buckets of human feces (collected by him and his eleven brothers) into the 1-A files at the Elk River draft board, in what became known as 'the Big Lake One' and is often cited as the first draft-board raid of the movement. He was convicted of destroying government property and interfering with the Selective Service and served about 14 months in federal prison.

On December 14, 1966, 18-year-old Cornell University SDS activist Bruce Dancis tore his draft card into four pieces before a crowd, then mailed the pieces to the Selective Service. His act helped inspire the April 1967 Central Park 'burn-in.' He was indicted and convicted of draft-card mutilation and served about 19 months in federal prison, entering in May 1969; he later wrote the memoir 'Resister.'

One of the youngest of the fifteen (Bill Durkin, age 19) who burned some 40,000 Chicago draft records on May 25, 1969. He was indicted on the four federal counts and was part of the group whose members served up to two years.

One of the youngest of the fifteen (Bill Sweeney, age 19) who broke into the Chicago Selective Service office and burned roughly 40,000 draft records on May 25, 1969. He was indicted on the four federal counts.

A Roman Catholic priest (Fr. John Pietra, age 33), he was one of the fifteen who burned some 40,000 Chicago draft records on May 25, 1969. He was indicted on four federal counts (destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy) and was among those convicted in June 1970, with sentences running up to two years.
At age 18 the youngest of the fifteen who burned Chicago draft records on May 25, 1969. He was indicted on the four federal counts alongside the group.

A Roman Catholic priest (Fr. Nick Riddell, age 39, the oldest of the group), he was one of the fifteen who burned Chicago draft records on May 25, 1969. He was indicted on the four federal counts and was among the ten convicted in June 1970; sentences for the group ran up to two years.
One of the fifteen (Charlie Muse, age 21) who burned some 40,000 Chicago draft records on May 25, 1969, and was indicted on the four federal counts.

A Jesuit seminarian (Society of Jesus) at the time, age 25, Mulligan was one of the fifteen who on May 25, 1969 broke into the Selective Service office at 2355 W. 63rd Street in Chicago, removed roughly 40,000 draft records and burned them in an alley, waiting to be arrested. He was among those convicted (10 of 11 tried were convicted in June 1970) and served prison time (group terms ran up to two years). Ordained a Jesuit priest in 1973, he spent decades as a liberation-theology missionary with Christian base communities in Nicaragua and wrote on the Jesuit martyrs of El Salvador.

A layperson and, at age 17, the youngest of the Silver Spring Three, Jon Bayless (brother of Les Bayless) took part in the May 21, 1969 destruction of several hundred draft records at the Silver Spring, Maryland Selective Service office, mutilating files with blood and paint and ransacking the office before waiting to be arrested. He was charged for his participation in the draft-board action; his specific sentence was not found.

Earl Leverette (also spelled Levrettes) was a member of the Milwaukee, Wisconsin chapter of the Black Panther Party and one of the "Milwaukee Three," arrested in September 1969 and charged with the attempted murder of a police officer along with Booker Collins and Jesse White. In September 1970, after the first morning of his trial, Leverette jumped bail and disappeared; he was later captured by FBI agents in Cincinnati, Ohio, and returned to Milwaukee in October 1971 at age 26. He was convicted and received a 10-year sentence, lighter than his two co-defendants.

William Lee Brent, born in Franklin, LA, joined the Black Panther Party at age 38 in 1968 making him the oldest member to join at the time. He was a devoted member of the Party and rose to the rank of captain, serving as a bodyguard for Eldridge Cleaver. In November 1968, Brent and two other Panthers in a van marked "Black Panther Black Community News Service" allegedly robbed a gas station in San Francisco's Bayview district of $80. Police cornered the three men and engaged in a shootout; in the process, a police officer was critically wounded. Brent was arrested, and before the trial could begin, he decided to hijack TWA Flight 154 on June 17th, 1969, redirecting the flight to Cuba. After the plane landed in Havana, Bill Brent was let off, and the plane soon returned to the United States. No one was injured. Brent was jailed in Cuba for 22 months before getting released and spending the rest of his life there. He earned a Spanish literature degree from the University of Havana, and taught English at various junior and senior high schools. In 1996, he published his own memoir called Long Time Gone: A Black Panther’s True-Life Story of His Hijacking and Twenty-Five Years In Cuba. He died in Cuba on November 4th at the age of 75 from pneumonia.

Felix Singer was a 32-year-old Freedom Rider from Chicago jailed at the Parchman state penitentiary in Mississippi in 1961. For their total passive resistance he and Terry Sullivan were dragged naked across concrete floors with 'wrist breakers' and shocked with electric cattle prods.

Miriam Feingold was a 20-year-old Swarthmore College student from Brooklyn who rode as a Freedom Rider in 1961 and spent 31 days in Mississippi jails — five at the Hinds County jail in Jackson and the rest at the Parchman state penitentiary — for testing interstate desegregation.

Terry Sullivan was a 19-year-old Freedom Rider from Chicago jailed at the Parchman state penitentiary in 1961. With Felix Singer he was subjected to 'wrist breakers' and electric cattle prods for refusing to cooperate with the segregated prison.

Barbara A. Thomas was a 21-year-old student at the Virginia Theological Seminary and College who served a 30-day jail term in Lynchburg in 1961 for a drugstore lunch-counter sit-in. She was also a lead petitioner in a suit challenging federal grants to segregated institutions.

Brenda Travis was a 16-year-old arrested in August 1961 in a sit-in at the McComb, Mississippi Greyhound bus station and sentenced to a year in reform school. Her punishment helped spark the October 1961 walkout by McComb high-school students.

Carolyn Long was a 20-year-old Clark College student and a spokesman for the sit-in group seated at Rich's restaurant during the October 1960 Atlanta department-store demonstrations, among the 73 arrested who refused to leave the whites-only counters.

Elizabeth Just was a 20-year-old New York University student sentenced to 30 days in the Women's House of Detention for defying New York's compulsory civil-defense drill on April 28, 1961 in an antinuclear protest.

John Artis was a 19-year-old with no criminal record, convicted alongside Carter; he stood by Carter's innocence and his own for decades.

On June 17, 1966, three people were shot to death at the Lafayette Bar and Grill in Paterson, New Jersey. Rubin "Hurricane" Carter, a nationally ranked middleweight boxer, and John Artis, a young man with no criminal record, were arrested and — on the testimony of two petty criminals, Alfred Bello and Arthur Bradley — convicted of the triple murder in 1967 and sentenced to life. No forensic evidence linked either man to the killings.

Bello and Bradley recanted in 1974, but a 1976 retrial again convicted both men. The case became an international cause célèbre — championed in Bob Dylan's 1975 song "Hurricane" and by a broad civil-rights and labor coalition — as an emblem of racist wrongful conviction. In November 1985, federal judge H. Lee Sarokin overturned the convictions, finding the prosecution had been "predicated upon an appeal to racism rather than reason, and concealment rather than disclosure." Carter was freed, and the charges were dismissed in 1988.

Linda Rosenstock was an 18-year-old arrested in the April 28, 1961 New York civil-defense-drill protest against nuclear-war preparations; she appeared in Adolescent Court and was paroled pending sentencing.

Ted Goertzel was an 18-year-old visiting Antioch College student arrested at Princeton in the April 28, 1961 civil-defense-drill protest when he refused to take cover during the nationwide 'Operation Alert.'

Woodrow Wilson Gillis was a Black man who, after being attacked by a white man and woman in Kinston, North Carolina in 1965 — the white man having pulled a knife on him — was himself convicted of assaulting the white couple and sentenced to 18 to 20 years on a North Carolina chain gang. He escaped and settled in the Germantown section of Philadelphia, living for years as a respected community member under the name Woodrow Wilson. In 1974, at age 51, he faced extradition back to North Carolina to serve at least 16 more years; his attorney David Kairys and his neighbors petitioned Pennsylvania Governor Milton Shapp not to send him back. Documented in The Black Panther (July 6, 1974).

Allan Hoffman was a 19-year-old artist and member of the Committee for Non-Violent Action sentenced to 60 days in the workhouse — then the harshest term ever imposed under the act — for refusing to take shelter during New York's compulsory civil-defense drill on April 28, 1961.

Bill Henry was a 27-year-old Committee for Non-Violent Action pacifist jailed with Donald Martin on trespassing charges after the two swam to and boarded the nuclear submarine Ethan Allen at its November 1960 launching in Groton, Connecticut, in the 'Polaris Action' protest against nuclear-missile submarines.

Donald Martin was a 20-year-old pacifist of the Committee for Non-Violent Action ('Polaris Action') who was jailed on trespassing charges after swimming out to and boarding the nuclear submarine Ethan Allen at its launching in Groton, Connecticut in November 1960, in protest against the Polaris missile program.

Edward Sanders was a 21-year-old Harvard student who, in the 1961 Polaris Action at New London, Connecticut, swam toward the nuclear submarine Thomas Edison in protest and was seized by Navy frogmen, among the eight pacifists sentenced.

Eugene Keyes was a 19-year-old New York University student and Committee for Non-Violent Action pacifist who, in the 1961 'Polaris Action' protest at Groton/New London, Connecticut, swam toward the nuclear submarine Thomas Edison before being seized by Navy frogmen. He was among eight sentenced for the protest.

Richard Zink was a 20-year-old Committee for Non-Violent Action pacifist sentenced in the 1961 Polaris Action protests against nuclear-missile submarines at New London, Connecticut; he was ordered to serve 30 days of a six-month term.

Dave Wyland, 23, of Toledo, Ohio, was one of the 'Omaha Action' pacifists who climbed over the fence at the Mead, Nebraska Atlas missile base in July 1959 to protest nuclear weapons, and was arrested for trespassing.

Ed Lazar, a 24-year-old New York City pacifist, was jailed for six months for antinuclear civil disobedience at the Mead, Nebraska intercontinental missile base in the July 1959 'Omaha Action' campaign.

Ross Anderson, 59, of Americus, Georgia, was one of the pacifists who in July 1959 climbed the fence at the Mead, Nebraska Atlas missile base with A. J. Muste in the 'Omaha Action' protest against nuclear weapons, and was arrested for trespassing.

Wilmer Young, a 71-year-old Quaker of Wallingford, Pennsylvania, was arrested for trespassing in July 1959 when he walked to the gate of the Mead, Nebraska intercontinental missile base in the 'Omaha Action' campaign of nonviolent protest against nuclear weapons.

Samuel Dashiell Hammett was the most influential American detective novelist of the twentieth century — the creator of the Continental Op, Sam Spade in The Maltese Falcon (1930), and Nick and Nora Charles in The Thin Man (1934). He was also a longtime member of the Communist Party USA, a U.S. Army veteran of two world wars (he enlisted at 48 in 1942 and served in the Aleutian Islands), and the longtime companion of playwright Lillian Hellman.

In 1946 Hammett accepted the role of trustee of the bail fund of the Civil Rights Congress, the CPUSA-aligned legal defense organization that posted bond for Smith Act defendants. When four of the original Dennis 11 defendants jumped bail in July 1951, Hammett was subpoenaed before the U.S. District Court in New York and ordered to identify the contributors to the bail fund. He refused, asserting that he did not know the contributors names and that even if he did he would not provide them. He was held in civil contempt and sentenced to six months in federal prison.

Hammett served his sentence at the Federal Correctional Institution camp at Ashland, Kentucky in 1951, where his health collapsed. After his release the IRS pursued him for back taxes for the rest of his life. He was blacklisted from publishing, magazine, and screenwriting work and never wrote another novel. He died of lung cancer in 1961, age 66, and was buried at Arlington National Cemetery as a U.S. Army veteran over the objection of J. Edgar Hoover.

Wesley Robert Wells was a Black California prisoner who became a national symbol of racist injustice after he was sentenced to death in 1947 for throwing a cuspidor — a metal spittoon — at a prison guard who had taunted him. No one was injured, but because Wells was already serving a life term as a "habitual criminal," assaulting a guard carried a mandatory death sentence. The Civil Rights Congress took up his case in 1948, with the radical attorney Charles Garry (later counsel to the Black Panther Party), winning a string of stays. In March 1954, two weeks before his scheduled execution, Governor Goodwin Knight commuted the death sentence to life. Wells spent almost his entire life behind bars before his release in 1974, and died about a year and a half later.

Longtime Black California prison activist and client of attorney Charles Garry, cited in The Black Panther Vol. 17 no.17 (1977) among the era's political prisoners. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v17 no.17; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

On July 1, 1974, at age 65, Wells was released on parole from the California Medical Facility at Vacaville after 47 years of confinement in California prisons, under the care of the Delancey Street Foundation. In a three-part interview with The Black Panther — whose attorney friend Charles Garry called him the original Panther — he described being sent to the STRESS psychiatric unit after 44 years inside, the 15-month parole denial that followed a clean bill of health, and his vow to keep struggling for prisoner rights (The Black Panther, August 10, 1974).

Martin Luther King Jr. was a prominent civil rights leader who developed nonviolent civil disobedience techniques during his leadership in the Montgomery Bus Boycott. King was arrested 29 separate times during the civil rights movement on spurious charges.

The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. was the 27-year-old president of the Montgomery Improvement Association when he was arrested and indicted under a 1921 Alabama anti-boycott statute for leading the Montgomery bus boycott against segregation. Tried in March 1956 — the test case for nearly 90 indicted boycotters — he was convicted and fined $500 while his home was bombed and the protest continued.

Hugo Butler was a Canadian-born American screenwriter (Lassie Come Home, The Southerner, Edison the Man) and one of the most prolific Hollywood blacklist exiles in Mexico. Subpoenaed by HUAC in 1951 he refused to testify and fled to Mexico City with his wife Jean Rouverol Butler and their five children. In Mexico he wrote screenplays for Luis Buñuel (Robinson Crusoe, 1954; The Young One, 1960) under pseudonyms and the front of producer George Pepper. He was a close friend and Mexican exile peer of Albert Maltz, Dalton Trumbo, and Elizabeth Catlett. He returned to the U.S. in the early 1960s and died of a stroke in Hollywood in 1968 at age 53.

William Mackie was a 49-year-old Portland, Oregon house painter who fought deportation from 1948 onward over alleged Communist Party membership in 1937–39. In 1958 Federal Judge Gus Solomon called the case 'outrageous' but refused to dismiss the deportation order; Mackie refused to identify associates.
Arsen Yerganian was a 67-year-old Armenian-born man ordered deported to Turkey in 1953. His case was part of the wave of McCarran-Walter Act deportation actions against foreign-born radicals.

Gus Polites was a 59-year-old Detroit restaurant and auto worker who had come from Greece in 1916. In 1958 he was fighting deportation on grounds that included his participation in unemployed demonstrations in the 1930s and his union organizing.

Thomas Dutton was a 70-year-old Detroit carpenter and railwayman, in the United States about 46 years, ordered deported to England in 1955 on the testimony of two paid informers that he had attended Communist meetings around 1929. The deportation was temporarily stayed under public pressure.

Charles Greenlee was the youngest of the Groveland Four — sixteen at the time — convicted in the 1949 Lake County, Florida rape case that became a national symbol of Jim Crow injustice. Spared the death penalty because of his age, he was sentenced to life imprisonment; he was paroled in 1962 and, with the others, posthumously pardoned in 2019 and exonerated in 2021.

One of the Groveland Four — four Black men accused on July 16, 1949 of raping 17-year-old Norma Padgett, a white woman, in Lake County, Florida — an accusation later proven false. Greenlee was 16 at arrest; sentenced to life imprisonment as a juvenile; paroled 1962. Officially exonerated by Florida courts in 2021.

One of the Trenton Six. The Trenton Six were six young Black men arrested February 11, 1948 and charged with the murder of William Horner, a 73-year-old white second-hand shop owner, on the basis of confessions extracted during 60+ hours of interrogation without counsel. After a 55-day trial in Mercer County Court, an all-white jury convicted all six on August 6, 1948 and sentenced them to death — a verdict the Civil Rights Congress and NAACP called a "Northern lynching." NJ Supreme Court reversed 1949; on retrial four were acquitted, Cooper pleaded guilty, and English was convicted with a life-sentence recommendation. English died in prison late 1952.

Billy Frank Jr. was a Nisqually fisherman and treaty-rights organizer first arrested in December 1945 at age 14 for fishing in the Nisqually River. He went on to be arrested more than fifty times through the 1960s and 1970s in defense of fishing rights guaranteed by the 1854 Treaty of Medicine Creek. From his family's six-acre property, Frank's Landing, he and Hank Adams organized the iconic LBJ-era 'fish-ins' modeled on the civil rights sit-ins, drawing the support of Marlon Brando (arrested 1964) and Dick Gregory. The arrests and protests culminated in the 1974 Boldt Decision (United States v. Washington), which restored Pacific Northwest tribes' rights to half the salmon harvest. Frank was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously in 2015.

Black defendant convicted in the racially asymmetric prosecutions following the June 1943 Detroit race riot — three days of white-mob violence against Black neighborhoods that killed 25 Black residents and 9 whites. President Roosevelt invoked the Insurrection Act and deployed federal troops to restore order. Of the 1,800 arrests that followed, 85% were of Black residents; nearly all rioting and assault prosecutions targeted Black defendants while white attackers were largely uncharged. Fox, age 17, was convicted of a riot-related murder he could not have committed; sentenced to 25 years. Cleared and released after a two-year legal fight by his defense team that exposed the prosecution's frame-up.

Reginald Thomas was a former International Labor Defense organizer sent to Sing Sing prison on a two-to-four-year sentence for a stabbing that New Masses (1941) reported he did not commit — eyewitnesses described a slight 17-year-old, while Thomas was 34 and heavyset. New Masses charged that he was prosecuted in retaliation for his earlier labor-defense organizing.

Alan Shaw was the 22-year-old Oklahoma City secretary of the Communist Party, arrested in August 1940 and held in the Oklahoma County Jail on $20,000 bond — spending his 22nd birthday in jail. Tried in December 1940, he was convicted and sentenced to ten years plus a $5,000 fine under the criminal-syndicalism law.

William Anderson was a 19-year-old assistant secretary of the Greenville, South Carolina NAACP branch and head of its youth council, arrested on a fabricated charge (using a school telephone to call a white girl), convicted, and sentenced to thirty days on the chain gang plus a $100 fine and $5,000 bond, amid a wave of Klan terror in Greenville.

David Butler was a 17-year-old Black Communist in Fort Lauderdale, Broward County, Florida, arrested on a trumped-up 'vagrancy' charge in a 1938 raid in which about fifteen Klan-affiliated police broke up a Communist Party meeting. Jailed and beaten with fists and blackjacks by Sheriff Walter Clark and a deputy to coerce testimony against his comrades, he was forced to repudiate his ILD lawyer and plead guilty, then fled town leaving a signed note exposing the coercion.

Rose Jackson was a 38-year-old white Communist Party organizer in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, arrested in the 1938 raid on a party meeting, handcuffed and marched through town to jail. Released without charge, she was re-arrested and jailed on a 'vagrancy' charge under $250 bond after issuing leaflets protesting the raid; the Fort Lauderdale defendants were eventually freed when the charges were dismissed.

Dolores 'Lolita' Lebrón Sotomayor led the four-person commando team that attacked the U.S. House of Representatives on March 1, 1954, shouting '¡Viva Puerto Rico libre!' from the visitors' gallery as she opened fire. She was 34 years old. Tried first in federal court in Washington and then in New York, she was sentenced to 56 years in federal prison and held at the Federal Reformatory for Women in Alderson, West Virginia, where she served 25 years before her sentence was commuted by President Carter in 1979. Returning to Puerto Rico, she remained a leading figure in the independence movement until her death in 2010, including a final imprisonment at age 81 for civil disobedience against the U.S. Navy bombing of Vieques.

On March 1, 1954, four members of the Puerto Rican Nationalist Party — Lolita Lebrón, Rafael Cancel Miranda, Andrés Figueroa Cordero, and Irvin Flores Rodríguez — entered the U.S. Capitol, took seats in the visitors' gallery overlooking the House chamber, unfurled a Puerto Rican flag, and opened fire on the Representatives below. Thirty rounds were fired in roughly thirty seconds; five Representatives were wounded but all survived. The attack was timed to draw international attention to the Inter-American Conference of the Organization of American States then opening in Caracas, and to challenge the U.S. claim that Puerto Rico had become a self-governing 'commonwealth.' All four were arrested at the scene, tried in federal court in Washington, D.C. and again in New York for related conspiracy charges, and sentenced to consecutive terms amounting effectively to life in federal prison. President Jimmy Carter commuted Andrés Figueroa Cordero's sentence in October 1977 (he was terminally ill with cancer and died in 1979); Carter commuted the remaining three sentences on September 6, 1979. They returned to Puerto Rico to a crowd estimated at 5,000 at San Juan International Airport.

Puerto Rican nationalist imprisoned for the 1954 armed protest inside the U.S. House of Representatives; The Black Panther Vol. 17 no.13 (1977) reports she and the other Nationalists refused to personally request pardons because doing so would imply accepting U.S. sovereignty over Puerto Rico. She was released in 1979. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v17 no.13; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

George Washington Henson was a 65-year-old union textile worker at Pelzer, South Carolina. During the 1935 textile strike he was first arrested for the murder of striker Gertrude Kelley — a charge dropped when the fatal bullet proved not to be from his shotgun — then indicted with eighteen others for rioting and jailed a week before making bond. Only strikers were jailed; none of those who fired on the strikers were arrested.

Ann Morton was a 23-year-old coal miner's daughter jailed in 1934 while leading an unemployed demonstration at the Sangamon County courthouse in Springfield, Illinois — one of many rank-and-file Unemployed Council activists arrested during the relief protests of the central-Illinois coalfields.

Frank Augusto, a 62-year-old striker in the 1928 New Bedford, Massachusetts textile strike, was beaten unconscious by police on the picket line and then sentenced to four months in jail — one of the elderly strikers whose treatment the ILD's Labor Defender publicized.

The Rev. Frank Dukes was a Birmingham civil-rights organizer and Miles College student leader who helped lay the groundwork for the 1963 Birmingham Campaign. As president of the Miles College Student Government Association he drafted the December 1961 statement "This We Believe" and led the 1962 Selective Buying Campaign, urging Black Birmingham residents to stop shopping at downtown businesses that kept segregated facilities or refused to hire Black workers in meaningful jobs; the resulting economic pressure desegregated some stores before Martin Luther King Jr. and the SCLC launched their better-known campaign. A co-leader of the 1963 Easter Sunday March — for which he was jailed — Dukes was active in the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights, the SCLC and the NAACP, and volunteered as one of Dr. King's Birmingham bodyguards. An Army veteran of the Korean War, he later became a minister, a vocational-rehabilitation counselor and a Miles College administrator. He died in Birmingham on November 11, 2023, aged 92.

John Thomas Scopes was a 24-year-old high-school teacher and football coach in Dayton, Tennessee when he was indicted on May 25, 1925 for violating the state's Butler Act, which banned the teaching of human evolution in public schools. The trial — orchestrated by the ACLU as a test case and known as the "Scopes Monkey Trial" — was held July 10-21, 1925 in Dayton. Clarence Darrow led the defense; William Jennings Bryan led the prosecution and famously took the stand to defend a literal reading of Genesis. Scopes was convicted and fined $100 by the trial judge. The Tennessee Supreme Court reversed in 1927 on the technical ground that the fine should have been imposed by the jury, leaving the Butler Act on the books (until its 1967 repeal) but vacating Scopes's conviction.

Ca'Quintez Gibson, 26, was charged with using the internet to incite a riot. He made a series of Facebook Live posts encouraging looting at Northwoods Mall and other locations in Peoria, IL: "It's going up tonight. Long as you all at Northwoods Mall. It's going up. Period... We ain't with that peaceful s---." Sentenced to 12 months probation; no incarceration.

A 16-year-old Black youth in Prince George's County, Maryland who, per The Black Panther Vol. 19 no.6,8 (1979), shot two police officers in self-defense after being beaten in custody; acquitted of first-degree murder but convicted of manslaughter and a handgun charge and sentenced to 25 years. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v19 no.6,8; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Ben Salmon was one of the most visible U.S. conscientious objectors of World War I, arguing from Catholic pacifist convictions that participation in war was morally impossible. On June 5, 1917, he wrote directly to President Wilson refusing to register for the draft on the grounds that all war was incompatible with the teachings of Christ; he was sentenced to death, which was reduced to 25 years hard labor for desertion and "spreading propaganda," and imprisoned at Fort Leavenworth. In 1920 he launched a hunger strike over his treatment and was transferred to St. Elizabeths Hospital; public pressure for the release of wartime objectors grew, and he was pardoned and freed in November 1920. His ordeal permanently broke his health; he died of pneumonia in 1932 at age 43.

Irwin St. John Tucker Born in Mobile, Alabama; Episcopal priest (ordained 1913, General Theological Seminary), Socialist Party member from 1912. Director of the SP National Office Literature Department in summer 1917, where he authored the antiwar pamphlet "The Price We Pay." Co-defendant in the Chicago Trial of Five. Conviction vacated by Berger v. US (1921). Served as priest-in-charge of St. Stephen's, Chicago (1927–1954); reinstated as Episcopal priest in 1970 at age 84.

William F. Kruse Appointed at age 21 by the SP National Executive Committee in July 1915 to direct the Young People's Socialist League; held that post through June 1918 and edited Young Socialists' Magazine. Youngest defendant in the Chicago Trial of Five; conviction vacated by Berger v. US (1921). Later worked in labor and film distribution (Amkino, importing Soviet films) and Communist Party-aligned organizations.

Howard Wilbur Moore New York farm laborer drafted in 1918 and sent to Camp Upton on April 29; refusing the uniform, was among about fifty-five "absolutists" transferred through Fort Riley and Camp Funston before arriving at Fort Leavenworth Disciplinary Barracks Armistice Day, November 11, 1918. Court-martialed and sentenced to five years' hard labor; beaten, hung by his thumbs, locked in vermin-infested cells, fed garbage, personally berated by visiting General John J. Pershing. Last absolutist released in late 1920. At age 95 wrote the lyrical memoir "Plowing My Own Furrow" (1985).

Mollie Steimer was an anarchist activist in New York City whose organizing centered on opposition to war, state repression, and the criminalization of radical speech. In August 1918 she distributed leaflets condemning U.S. intervention against revolutionary Russia and calling on workers to resist militarism; she was arrested and later convicted under wartime sedition laws, receiving a 15-year prison sentence and a fine. After further arrests and a prolonged legal battle culminating in Abrams v. United States, her sentence was ultimately commuted on the condition of deportation, and she was expelled from the country in 1921. She continued political activity abroad, including advocacy for anarchist prisoners, reflecting a life shaped by both activism and forced exile.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Born 1897, Dunaivtsi, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Jewish. Garment worker. Migrated to US 1912, with parents and four siblings. Began working immediately after arrival, at age 16. Became an anarchist after discovering the writings of Peter Kropotkin; 1917 became a member of New York’s militant Jewish anarchist Shturem Group, which in 1918 became the Frayhayt Group. Arrested, with Hyman Lachowsky, while distributing radical leaflets protesting US intervention in the Russian Civil War on August 23, 1918. While out on bail, arrested eleven more times over eight months, including during a raid on the Union of Russian Workers’ People’s House in New York during the first Palmer Raids in November 1919. Convicted, with other members of the Frayhayt Group, for violation of the Espionage Act, and sentenced to 15 years in prison; after losing landmark Supreme Court free-speech case Abrams v. United States, sentence commuted on the condition of deportation. While detained on Ellis Island awaiting deportation, led a hunger strike to protest her segregation from other detainees. According to a supervisor, “Certainly it would not be safe to put her in a room with other detained females, this by reason of her known activities in spreading the propaganda of anarchism among among women and girls. Most of those detained female aliens will probably be admitted to the United States in due course, and to permit Mollie Steimer to sow the seeds of anarchism among them while they are the wards of the Government would be highly improper.” Deported November 1, 1921. 

In Russia, almost immediately involved in aid work for imprisoned anarchists; through this work she met her companion Senya Fleshin, an anarchist who had voluntarily returned from the US in 1917, and together they founded the Society to Help Anarchist Prisoners (with financial aid from comrades in the US). November 1922 both were arrested for this work and sentenced to two years internal exile in Siberia, but released after launching a hunger strike. Both arrested again July 9, 1923, for propagating anarchist ideas. Launched an eight-day hunger strike along with other political prisoners, including several other deportees from the US; Steimer and Fleshin given visas to Germany with the understanding that they would be executed if they returned to Russia, and left September 27, 1923. In Berlin, then after 1924 in Paris, the pair worked with Emma Goldman, Alexander Berkman, and other exiled Russian anarchists to aid radicals imprisoned in Russia. Steimer corresponded with, and was regularly visited by, anarchists from the US and elsewhere. In 1939 Steimer organized aid for refugees from the Spanish Civil War who had been placed in French internment camps; in May 1940, with the Nazi occupation of Paris, Steimer was herself sent to the internment camp in Gurs for seven weeks. After her release, she and Fleshin fled to Mexico, where they were aided by fellow deportees Jacob and Mary Abrams. Active in radical and exile circles in Mexico City, where they befriended Diego Rivera and Spanish anarchist exiles, and Fleshin ran a photography studio. Remained in constant correspondence with anarchists abroad. Steimer died of heart attack July 23, 1980 in Cuernavaca.

Margaret E. Cornell was an Irish-born office clerk, age 52 at the time of her conviction, who worked at the German Consulate in San Francisco. She was the only woman convicted in the federal Hindu-German Conspiracy trial (formally the Indo-German-Irish plot to ship American weapons to India for an uprising against British rule and to disrupt British and Allied munitions shipping during World War I). Federal prosecutors charged her under Sections 13 and 37 of the U.S. criminal code with espionage and conspiracy for transmitting coded messages between her boss, Consul-General Franz Bopp, and Charles C. Crowley, a private detective hired by the consulate. At trial she testified, I am now a woman without a country. Whether she was a willing participant or a low-level clerical dupe was disputed. Her trial drew heavy press coverage and her mug shot was reproduced in Butterick's Delineator (July 1918) in the gallery of Huns, Spies and Traitors. The San Quentin admission record dated February 8, 1918 lists her as Margaret E. Cornell, occupation office clerk, age 52, birthplace Ireland. She had Irish-Republican sympathies, and the 1916 Easter Rising is part of the political context of her case. Cornell told the court she had tuberculosis and feared dying in prison; her ultimate fate is not well documented in surviving newspaper records.

William Breidert was a conscientious objector from New York imprisoned during World War I. Court-martialed for refusing military service, he was held at Fort Douglas. Sentenced to 30 years in prison - reduced to 2 years. (Documented in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection's World War I Conscientious Objectors database.) Archival note: registered for the draft on June 5, 1917 as a CO, at age 24; taken to Ft. Jay, transferred to Camp Upton; classified as a 3, later as a 7; refused to wear uniform; interviewed by the Special Bd. …

LeRoy Pinkett Pvt. LeRoy Pinkett, age 23 at conviction, was found guilty of murder, mutiny, and assault with intent to murder in one of the Houston court-martials and was imprisoned at Fort Leavenworth. Conviction set aside November 2023.

John Reed was an American journalist and revolutionary, best known for his eyewitness account of the 1917 Russian Revolution, Ten Days That Shook the World. He was a contributor to The Masses and a co-defendant with Max Eastman in the November 1917 federal indictment under the Espionage Act for conspiracy to obstruct military recruitment. The first trial (April 1918) ended in a hung jury; the second (October 1918) also ended in a hung jury, and the charges were dismissed. In 1919 Reed co-founded the Communist Labor Party of America in Chicago and was indicted in absentia on sedition charges by Illinois state authorities under the criminal-syndicalism statute. He fled to Soviet Russia, where he died of typhus in Moscow on October 19, 1920 at age 32. Reed is one of only three Americans buried at the Kremlin Wall Necropolis.

Thomas Mooney San Francisco labor organizer and IWW militant — son of an Irish coal-miner Knights of Labor organizer — who along with Warren K. Billings was framed for the July 22, 1916 Preparedness Day Parade bombing on Market Street that killed ten and injured forty. Convicted of first-degree murder in 1917 on perjured testimony; sentenced to death. President Wilson, alarmed that Mooney's execution might trigger Russian-style worker revolt, personally interceded with California Governor William Stephens, who in 1918 commuted the sentence to life. The case became a 22-year international cause célèbre. Pardoned by Governor Culbert L. Olson on January 7, 1939. Thomas Mooney was San Francisco labor leader and socialist activist. On July 22, 1916, a parade was organized in San Francisco by local supporters of the Preparedness Movement which advocated American entry into World War I. A suitcase bomb was detonated by an unknown assailant, killing 10. Mooney and labor leader Warren Billings were both framed for the bombing by the San Francisco Police Department using falsified evidence and perjured testimony from a paid off witness, Frank Oxman. On November 1920, Draper Hand of the SFPD went to Mayor James Rolph and admitted that he had helped Charles Fickert and Martin Swanson frame Mooney. Later, two witnesses, Edgar Rigall and Earl K. Hatcher, came forward and provided evidence that Frank Oxman was 200 miles away during the bombing and could not have seen what he told the court at the trial of Mooney. In February 1921, John McDonald confessed that the police had forced him to lie about the planting of the bomb. Despite this new evidence the Californian authorities refused a retrial. Mooney served 22 years in prison before finally being pardoned in 1939 by Governor Culbert Olson. By then, Mooney had been suffering from jaundice and ulcers from his time and prison and died shortly after in 1942 at age 59.

Frank Tannenbaum was a 21-year-old Austrian-born IWW unemployed-workers' organizer in New York City during the brutal winter of 1913-14. In March 1914 he led a band of homeless men into St. Alphonsus Catholic Church on West Broadway demanding food and shelter, in the most famous of his 'army of the unemployed' church occupations. Convicted of unlawful assembly, he served one year on Blackwell's Island and went on to become a distinguished Columbia historian of Latin America and U.S. labor.

Mary Harris Jones Mary G. Harris Jones — known the world over as "Mother" Jones — was an Irish-born American labor organizer whose half-century of agitation against industrial exploitation made her, in the words of a West Virginia federal prosecutor in 1902, "the most dangerous woman in America." Born in Cork, Ireland in 1837, she emigrated as a child with her family during the Irish famine, settling first in Canada and later in the United States, where she trained as a dressmaker and a schoolteacher. In 1867 her husband, an iron moulder and union member, and all four of their children died in the yellow fever epidemic that swept Memphis. Four years later she lost her dressmaking shop and everything she owned in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. From those losses she built a new life entirely inside the labor movement, traveling town to town in support of striking workers and helping organize miners, garment workers, steelworkers, and railroad employees. From 1900 onward she focused on the coalfields, organizing for the United Mine Workers of America in West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Colorado. In 1903 she led the "March of the Mill Children" from Kensington, Pennsylvania to Theodore Roosevelt's home on Long Island to demand laws against child labor. In 1905 she was one of the founders of the Industrial Workers of the World. She was a powerful public speaker who built her organizing around the families of striking miners — and was repeatedly jailed for it. During the Paint Creek–Cabin Creek strike in West Virginia in February 1913, she was arrested at age 75, tried by a military commission under martial law, and sentenced to twenty years in the state penitentiary on charges of conspiracy to commit murder. Held under house arrest at a boarding house in Pratt, West Virginia, she contracted pneumonia and was nearly killed. After 85 days a U.S. Senate investigation into conditions in the West Virginia coalfields — opened in direct response to her case — forced her release. Months later she traveled to Colorado to organize miners against the Rockefeller-owned Colorado Fuel and Iron Company in what became known as the Colorado Coalfield War. She was arrested again in early 1914, held without charge in the San Rafael Hospital and the Mount San Rafael jail in Trinidad, and ultimately escorted out of the state by the militia. Her imprisonment in Colorado ended only weeks before company gunmen and National Guard troops attacked the strikers' tent colony at Ludlow, killing more than 20 people including women and children. She continued organizing into her nineties. She published her Autobiography of Mother Jones in 1925 and died on November 30, 1930, at the age of 93, at a farm outside Washington, D.C. She is buried at the Union Miners Cemetery in Mount Olive, Illinois, alongside the miners killed in the 1898 Virden massacre. Her name endures on union halls, on a magazine, and in the labor movement's most cited rallying cry — her own: "Pray for the dead, and fight like hell for the living."

Elizabeth Gurley Flynn was one of the most consequential American radicals of the twentieth century. As a teenage organizer in the early 1900s she became a leading figure of the Industrial Workers of the World, leading textile, silk, and miners strikes from Lawrence, Massachusetts to Paterson, New Jersey to the Mesabi iron range — Joe Hills 1915 song The Rebel Girl was written for her. She was a co-founder of the American Civil Liberties Union in 1920 and remained on its board until 1940, when she was expelled in a closed vote because of her membership in the Communist Party USA, a vote the ACLU formally apologized for in 1976.

In June 1951 she was indicted in the Foley Square Second String — the federal governments second wave of Smith Act prosecutions, which targeted thirteen members of the CPUSA national board after the original Dennis 11. Convicted at trial in early 1953, she was sentenced to three years in federal prison and began her sentence at the Federal Reformatory for Women at Alderson, West Virginia, in January 1955 at age 64. She served 28 months and was released in May 1957. Her prison memoir The Alderson Story: My Life as a Political Prisoner appeared in 1963. She became national chairwoman of the Communist Party USA in 1961, a position she held until her death in Moscow in 1964.

Louis Lingg was a 22-year-old German-born carpenter and the youngest of the Haymarket defendants. He had not been at the rally and prosecutors did not allege he was — they argued only that he had built bombs. On the night of November 10, 1887, the eve of his scheduled execution, he killed himself in his cell with a smuggled blasting cap, denying the state his execution.

On May 4, 1886, a rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square in support of an eight-hour workday and against the police killing of striking workers at the McCormick Reaper plant the previous day was nearing its end when an unknown assailant threw a bomb into a column of police advancing to disperse the crowd. The explosion and the police gunfire that followed killed seven officers and at least four civilians. Eight Chicago anarchist organizers were arrested and tried together for the bombing, although no evidence ever connected most of them to the device or the bomb-thrower. The 1886 trial, presided over by Judge Joseph Gary, was widely condemned at the time and since as a political prosecution. Four were hanged on November 11, 1887; one died in his cell the night before the executions. Three years later, on June 26, 1893, Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld pardoned the three surviving prisoners and issued a long public statement excoriating the trial as a miscarriage of justice. The case helped establish May 1 as International Workers' Day around the world.

Jack Gaveel was born 1889 in Amsterdam, Netherlands.

Migrated to England in 1905; returned to the Netherlands in 1910 and emigrated to Canada that same year. Joined the IWW in 1913 in Canada and became secretary of IWW Local no. 339 in Edmonton, Canada the following year. Migrated to the U.S. in 1915. Included in the federal indictment of IWW leaders in 1917, but dropped from the case before it went to trial. Acted as an IWW delegate in Los Angeles, where he was “active in organizing the Austrian and Croatian fishermen.” Arrested in April 1921 and sentenced to 1-4 years under California’s criminal syndicalism law. In San Quentin, refused to work in the prison jute mill, declaring: “I have never scabbed on my class outside of prison, and I won’t do it inside.” He was sent to solitary confinement, sparking a sympathy strike of thirteen other imprisoned IWW members. Deported to The Netherlands on August 1, 1924.

Remained active in labor and anarchist circles in The Netherlands. Into 1951 he resumed contact with the IWW and distributed IWW materials in Europe. In 1960, at age 71, he wrote: “I wish I were in America. I’d join you in the fight then.”

Sam Povff was born 1878 in Poltava, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Immigrated to the United States in 1910.

An anarchist since age 17. Arrested in 1899 for revolutionary activities but released. Later claimed he participated in a mutiny at the Kronstadt naval base and was sentenced to 13 years’ internal exile in Siberia, from which he escaped. 

In the United States he briefly belonged to an anarchist organization in New York, then moved to the West Coast where he used numerous aliases and supported himself through apparently politically motivated theft. Arrested 1911 in Huntington, Oregon for larceny (receiving a two-year sentence); circa 1912 in Stockton for burglary (two years in San Quentin State Prison); and 1914 in Los Angeles for highway robbery (a six-year sentence, of which he served four years and two months). Arrested again in Portland in 1919 for attempted robbery of moonshine sellers, explaining “They had no right to poison the working class people. I think I had a right to rob them.” Immigration authorities called him “a most reprehensible and undesirable character.” Deported to Russia December 17, 1922.

Black man held in Boston federal custody under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 after escaping from enslavement in Virginia. His May 1854 arrest in Boston touched off the largest abolitionist protests of the antebellum era — an estimated 50,000 people lined the streets to witness his court-ordered return to slavery, the federal government deploying state militia and U.S. Marines to enforce the rendition. Defended by Richard Henry Dana Jr. and Charles Mayo Ellis. After return to Virginia, abolitionists purchased his freedom; he later became a Baptist minister in Ontario, Canada, where he died of tuberculosis in 1862 at age 28.

Charles Holt was an American printer and editor and the publisher of the Bee in New London, Connecticut, the leading Democratic-Republican newspaper in southeastern Connecticut. He had been a journeyman printer in New York before founding the Bee in 1797 at age 24 specifically as a Jeffersonian counter-weight to the Federalist Connecticut Gazette.

In May 1799 Holt published an editorial attacking the Federalist administration's military buildup against France, in particular the recruitment of a "standing army" he depicted as a tool to suppress political opposition at home. He was indicted under the Sedition Act in September 1799 and tried before Justice Bushrod Washington (nephew of George Washington) in Hartford in April 1800. The federal jury convicted him; he was sentenced to three months in the New London jail and a \$200 fine. After his release he continued the Bee for several more years and later moved to New York to edit the Columbian. Holt's case is one of the most cited Sedition Act prosecutions because the underlying editorial was specifically about whether peacetime conscription threatened civil liberties — a theme that has resurfaced in every American war debate since.

Revolutionary War major (4th Pennsylvania Battalion) and Mingo Creek militia commander during the Whiskey Rebellion. Led the rebel force of roughly 600 western Pennsylvania farmers that besieged federal tax inspector John Neville's fortified home at Bower Hill on July 17, 1794. Killed by a Neville-side sniper during a parley flag; his death enraged the rebels, who then burned Bower Hill, and was the proximate trigger for Washington's federalization of 13,000 militia and the Insurrection Act invocation that crushed the rebellion. Martyred at age 43.
